Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, you are tasting the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And you are not recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾

In the preceding verses, Allah, may He be glorified, related the speech of the followers (al-mutbi'un) to their leaders, the wrongdoers (al-zalimun):

﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed, we are going to taste [punishment].﴾ [al-Saffat: 31] Here He emphasizes this same meaning, except that He specifies here the type of tasting: ﴿you are tasting the painful punishment.﴾ This painful punishment is not an injustice or a transgression; rather, it is the recompense for what you had put forward: ﴿And you are not recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ [al-Saffat: 39]

You are tasting the painful punishment. And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.

In the preceding verses, He—glorified is He—related the words of the wrongdoers spoken by their leaders to their followers:

"So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed, we are tasting [it]" (Al-Saffat: 31). Here this meaning is affirmed, except that it specifies here the kind of tasting: "Indeed, you are tasting the painful punishment" (Al-Saffat: 38). And this painful punishment is not an injustice or transgression; rather, it is the recompense for what you have put forward: "And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verses 40–45:

The discussion of the reward of the disbelievers has already passed. Here comes an exception: ﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 40]. They are excluded and far removed from this fate. The word ﴿chosen﴾ [al-Saffat: 40] is the plural of mukhlas (one whom Allah has purified and singled out), with fatha on the lam, so it is a passive participle (ism maf'ul). It means those whom Allah has purified and chosen for His obedience and worship. ﴿For them is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat: 41], that is, in the Hereafter, because the provision of this world is not known. You toil and exert yourself in this world, and you may be deprived of the fruit of that toil: the crop may fail and the trade may suffer loss.

So, we have a provision in this world, but it is not known. As for the Hereafter, your provision is known, specified for you, and never fails; no causes stand between you and it, because in the Hereafter you live, as we have said, with the One who causes all causes, glorified is He.

We have already defined provision (rizq) and said that it is everything from which one benefits, even what is taken unlawfully is counted as provision. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172].

Then the context moves on to detail what was summarized in the word "provision". The most important provision from which a person benefits is the necessary sustenance by which his life subsists, then the enjoyment of what refines this life. But here the Truthful, glorified is He, did not mention the necessities; He mentioned the luxury beyond the necessities: ﴿fruits, and they will be honoured﴾ [al-Saffat: 42], although in other places He mentioned the necessities and then followed them with fruits and luxuries, such as His saying: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit and what their hands have made. Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 35].

So why is the discussion here limited to fruit alone? They said: because the discussion here concerns the Hereafter, and eating in the Hereafter is not out of need for food, but is pleasure and enjoyment of eating. Or: the meaning is that since Allah has guaranteed you enjoyment, then by greater measure He has guaranteed you the necessary sustenance.

The meaning of ﴿and they will be honoured﴾ [al-Saffat: 42] is that food is not thrown to them so that they may eat, as we throw grass to animals, for example; we do not intend thereby to honour them. Rather, this provision is brought to them ﴿and they will be honoured. In gardens of delight﴾ [al-Saffat: 42-43], because it is the provision of a lover to his beloved.

His saying: ﴿upon couches facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 44] means that He does not burden them with the hardship of visiting one another. The couches on which they sit face each other, so that if you wish to visit a brother of yours, you find him in front of you without having to move to him. This is a guaranteed matter.

﴿A cup from a flowing spring is passed around among them﴾ [al-Saffat: 45]. In another verse, He explained who passes around this cup: ﴿There will go around them youths made eternal, with cups and ewers and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17-18].

The cup (ka's) is meant to refer to the wine or the vessel in which the wine is placed. ﴿From a flowing spring﴾ [al-Saffat: 45] means: from something you see with your eyes, or from springs that flow as water springs flow. Then He describes this wine as (white), and white is the purest kind of wine according to the Arabs.

﴿A delight for the drinkers﴾ [al-Saffat: 46]. He did not say "delicious" (ladhidhah) but "a delight" (ladhdhah), that is, it is in its very essence a delight, as if delight has become embodied in this cup, just as you say: so-and-so is just (adil). If you want to intensify this description, you say: so-and-so is justice ('adl).

The description of the wine of the Hereafter as ﴿a delight for the drinkers﴾ [al-Saffat: 46] is to distinguish it from the wine of this world, because the wine of this world, as we see them drinking it in films, is not drunk for pleasure. One pours a little of it into the cup, then pours it into his mouth, and takes it reluctantly because of the dislike of its taste.

But since the wine of this world holds no pleasure in its consumption, why do they drink it? They drink it for the effect that arises from it, the disturbance of the mind which serves as a guard over movement, and they want to be free and liberated from this guard. Therefore, the finest kind of wine among them, God forbid, is the one that takes him out of his consciousness and does to him such-and-such.

As for the wine of the Hereafter, it shares with this only its name. The wine of the Hereafter is a delight that you feel when you take it, and you drink it sip by sip, slowly, to savour its sweetness; and it does not take away the mind or ruin it: ﴿neither is there in it intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47], that is, it does not ruin the minds or take them away.

﴿Nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. It is said: "nazafa al-hawd" (he drained the basin), meaning he emptied it of water gradually to its end. And "nazafa al-dam" means the blood flowed from the body drop by drop until the person dies.

Among kinds of wine is that which causes a draining of what is in the belly, so that its drinker empties everything in his stomach and expels all that is in his insides. But the wine of the Hereafter does not cause this draining.

Or the meaning of ﴿nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47] is that their minds are not drained, and they do not become drunk because of it, as the wine of this world intoxicates.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 41:

﴿أُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمْ رِزْقٌ مَّعْلُومٌ﴾ means: in the Hereafter, because the provision of this world is not known, since you toil and exert yourself in this world, and you may be deprived of the fruit of this toil. The farming may be ruined, and the trade may suffer loss.

So: we have a provision in this world, but it is not known. As for the Hereafter, your provision is known, specified for you, and never fails, nor do causes stand between you and it, because you live in the Hereafter, as we have said, with the Causer (al-Musabbib), glorified is He.

We have already defined provision (rizq) and said: it is everything that one benefits from...

This is a description of the women of Paradise: they are "qāṣirāt al-ṭarf" (restraining the gaze), meaning that she lowers her gaze and does not look at anyone other than her husband...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verse 49:

This is a description of the women of Paradise, for they are ﴿qāṣirāt al-ṭarf..﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 48], meaning: they lower their gaze, so they do not look at anyone other than their husbands. We have said that the most precious thing a person possesses may be given by him to another: you lend your friend your car, for example, or your house, or your garment... etc.

As for the woman, she is the one thing that does not accept even a mere glance at her, because of her privacy and her standing. Likewise, you love that your wife's eye not extend to others besides you. These are among the attributes of the people of Paradise: they are ﴿qāṣirāt al-ṭarf..﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 48], restricting their gaze to their husbands. And they are, as in another verse: ﴿ḥūrun maqṣūrātun fī al-khiyām﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 72], meaning: confined and guarded for their husbands.

So Allah, glorified is He, safeguards the beauty of woman and is keen on a chaste formation within society, so that offspring come forth noble and pure. And these standards that the believing woman has in this world are also so in the Hereafter. It is as if Allah, glorified is He, reassures husbands regarding this privacy, and affirms that the wife in it is not shared by anyone, not even by a glance.

The meaning of ﴿ʿīn﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 48] is the plural of ʿaynāʾ, meaning: wide-eyed with beautiful eyes. This is among the signs of grace and beauty in a woman according to the Arabs; therefore, among the standards they set for beauty is that the eye should be wide and the mouth small, such that if her eye were measured against her mouth, her eye would be wider.

The meaning of (ʿindahum), i.e., in their possession, because they are among the provisions of Paradise: whoever desires something from them finds it, and otherwise he refrains from it, but it is present with them.

Then He describes them, glorified is He, with His words: ﴿ka-annahunna bayḍun maknūn﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 49]. The word ﴿bayḍ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 49] is the plural of bayḍa, and what is meant is ostrich eggs, because they are larger and more beautiful in color. They say of one who protects the camels in his tribe: he protects its egg; therefore the eggs are described here as ﴿maknūn﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 49], meaning guarded, protected, concealed, to which no hand has been extended.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verses 50–53:

We have already listened to a dialogue that took place between the guilty disbelievers in the Fire.

Here, the Truth, glorified is He, relates to us this dialogue among the people of Paradise, who ask about the people of wrongdoing, of error and misguidance, and of denial: where are they now, and what is their fate?

﴿Said one of them﴾ [al-Saffat: 51], from among the people of Paradise, ﴿"Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ [al-Saffat: 51], i.e., a companion in the worldly life, ﴿who used to say, "Are you really among those who affirm?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 52], i.e., affirm the Resurrection, ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be recompensed?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 53], meaning: will we be called to account? This question from him was by way of denial and rejection of the matter of the Resurrection and the Reckoning.

The Qur'an portrays this scene for you as though you were seeing it, and relates it as though you were hearing it. While the people of Paradise are busy asking one another about the people of misguidance, those whom they used to know in the world, one of them looks and catches sight of the people of the Fire. He sees his companion who tried to lead him astray, the one who denied resurrection and reckoning.

So he says to those sitting with him: "Look at him, so-and-so, in the Fire."

﴿So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55], i.e., in its middle, so there is no hope for him of being saved from it. Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verses 62–65:

The verses here alternate between mention of Paradise and its delights, and mention of the Fire and its punishment. They return once more to Hell, its torment, and a description of what is in it. ﴿Is that﴾ [al-Saffat: 62], i.e., what has been mentioned before of the delights of Paradise, ﴿better﴾ [al-Saffat: 62], more excellent; so it carries the sense of the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil). ﴿Nuzulan﴾ [al-Saffat: 62], i.e., a dwelling place and hospitality.

The nuzul is what is prepared for an unexpected guest of lodging, containing the means of life, such as food, drink and other things; for this reason they call the hotel (nuzul). Hotels, with all the comforts found in them now, are what humans have prepared for humans, so how can you conceive of what the Lord of humankind has prepared? Hospitality must necessarily be in proportion to the capacity of the host.

﴿Or the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Saffat: 62]. It is natural for us to ask: what is the tree of zaqqum, O Lord? So God describes it to us: ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Saffat: 63]. Fitnah (trial) means: an ordeal and punishment. ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 64], i.e., in its midst.

This is one manifestation of the absoluteness of divine power. Do not ask how a tree can grow in the middle of the fire, because the Doer is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So take it within the framework of the transcendence of the Truth above the laws of creation.

The meaning of ﴿its shoots﴾ [al-Saffat: 65] is its fruit. ﴿As if they were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65]. But we have not seen the heads of devils. Therefore some orientalists who try to find fault with the words of God have stood up and said:

How does God in this verse liken an unknown to an unknown? We have not seen the tree of zaqqum, nor have we seen the heads of devils. A simile comes to clarify the likened by mentioning the thing it is likened to, so what is the benefit of likening an unknown to an unknown?

We say: the human brain has a part for retention, a part for memory, and a part for imagination called mukhayyilah. A person sees things, and retention records them in the margin of consciousness; then memory recalls these things for him. As for imagination, it takes from the reality of things and forms new imagined images that have no basis in reality.

Here, with this simile, ﴿its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65], although you have not seen the heads of devils, your imagination will draw for them an image in the most hideous form possible, and then the difference will become clear to you between the hospitality which God has prepared for the believers in Paradise and this tree whose fruit is like the heads of devils. The combining of these two images is intended, for your Lord, Mighty and Majestic, wished to present to you admonition at the time of the witnessed recompense, not at the time of denial.

The tree of zaqqum is a wicked tree, foul of smell, bitter of taste, found in the region of Tihamah. God made it an example of the tree that grows at the root of the Hellfire. They said: this is a rebuke to those tormented by this tree, because they used to deny resurrection and life after death. So God made for them this tree growing in the midst of Hell, and in it is their food, so they have no taste except its fruit.

The word shajarah (tree) implies greenness and water, and it is known that water is contrary to fire. In this is an indication of the absoluteness of power which they denied in the world. So: that this tree is at the root of Hell, while they live on its fruit and need it, and it stands before them in plain view, all of this is a rebuke to them for what they denied.

This matter reminds us of our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he was cast into the fire, and God made it cool and safe for him, and by His power, exalted is He, suspended the law of burning.

The Truth, glory be to Him, wishes to make the image of this tree hideous, although the Arabs know a tree by this name, and know its wickedness, the stench of its smell, and the bitterness of its taste, and know its simple shoots; but no one has seen a shoot resembling the heads of devils.

So: the intent is to make it hideous and to give imagination the opportunity to go in every direction in imagining its ugliness. The shoot of every thing is beautiful; indeed it is the most beautiful part of the tree. But this one's shoot is as if it were the heads of devils, and you may imagine what it contains of ugliness, deformity, and repulsive form.

It is known that the Arabs believed devils to be the most hideous in form, and the angel to be the most beautiful and handsome in form. Among this is the saying of the women when they saw Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿Allah forbid! This is no human; this is none but a noble angel﴾ [Yusuf: 31].

So: the Qur'an, in this simile, took into account the beliefs of the Arabs, and came with an unknown image. Yes, but each person will imagine it according to the measures of ugliness in his own mind. Had it come with a specific, known example of ugliness, it would have been of one hue, and perhaps it would be ugly in the eyes of one person and not ugly in the eyes of another. But the Truth, glory be to Him, wants a repulsive sight in the eyes of all. Which of us imagines the devil as beautiful?

Therefore we said: if we brought caricaturists from around the world, and told them: draw for us an imagined picture of the devil, each of them would draw an image of ugliness in his own view, and you would not find in them one image like another. So: the likening of the shoot of the tree of zaqqum to the heads of devils came to spread all meanings of ugliness among souls, and this image is sufficient to make us repelled by this tree.

The original meaning of ṭalʿ is the sheath that contains the first fruit of the tree, and it is also said of the spathe that contains the fruit of the date palm and similar things. When its strands emerge and its roundness and formation become clear, it is called (balah) as long as it is green in colour.

The balah has three attributes:

The first: its size. When it takes its natural and final size, it appears without colour, and then it turns either red or yellow. At this stage they say (al-balah ʿaffar) and call it (zahw).

The second: when the colour settles and its redness or yellowness is complete, they call it (busr).

The third attribute: after size and colour comes texture, soft or dry according to the environment. If the environment is hot and dry, it affects the busr and dries it, so it becomes dates (tamr); and if the environment is cold and humid, the busr becomes rutab.

The second: when the colour settles and its redness or yellowness is complete, they call it (busr).

The third attribute: after size and colour comes texture, soft or dry according to the environment. If the environment is hot and dry, it affects the busr and dries it, so it becomes dates (tamr); and if the environment is cold and humid, the busr becomes rutab.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 66:

﴿Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, upon it they will have a mixture of boiling water.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, their return will be to the Blazing Fire.﴾

Meaning: Necessity will compel them and force them to this bitter, distressing food, since they will have no other food. ﴿Indeed, they will eat from it﴾, and they will not eat only to the measure of necessity; rather, ﴿they will fill their bellies with it﴾. When they fill their bellies with it, the fire within them increases, so they will seek a drink to extinguish this fire, and their drink will be boiling water (ḥamīm), and we seek refuge in Allah.

The meaning is: necessity will compel them and force them toward this bitter, distressing food, since they will have no other food. ﴿Indeed they will eat from it﴾ [al-Saffat: 66], and they will not eat only as much as necessity requires. Rather, ﴿they will fill their bellies with it﴾ [al-Saffat: 66]. When they fill their bellies with it, the Fire within them increases, so they will seek a drink to quench this fire, and their drink will be ḥamīm (scalding water), and we seek refuge in Allah.

﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of ḥamīm﴾ [al-Saffat: 67]. The shawb is that which is mixed and blended, and the ḥamīm is water that has reached the utmost degree of heat. In another place, the Qur'an calls it ghislīn (a foul discharge of the people of Hell). This is their drink, and we seek refuge in Allah. When they have eaten and drunk, they return to Hellfire again: ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 68].

Then the Truthful One, glorified is He, explains the cause of this, the reason for this painful end, and that it is not an injustice to them, but rather the recompense for what they did:

﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 69:

Meaning: "They found their fathers astray." ﴿So they are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Saffat: 70]. Meaning: they follow their way and imitate them. As for the meaning of ﴿yuhra'un﴾ [al-Saffat: 70] (يُهْرَعُونَ), it means they are driven and hasten, as if something were compelling them to hurry. This is because the verb (yuhra'un) is in the passive voice, i.e., because its doer is not named, as we say: "So-and-so was seized (zukima fulan)," where the doer is unknown.

Had the hastening in following the fathers come from them, it would have been said "yahra'un" with a fatha. Rather, "yuhra'un" [indicates that] as if something pushes them to imitate the fathers, to show you, glory be to Him, that evil is more contagious, because there is no restraint of the self in it and no check on desire. Therefore a person runs toward it and hastens in seeking it.

As for guidance and the method, a person does not hasten toward it, because it narrows down the field of desires for him and restricts his movement within the framework of what God has legislated. So the upshot is: they imitate the fathers while knowing that they are astray, in order to escape the bond of the legal obligations.

Therefore, when God, exalted is He, took the covenant from us while we were in the world of atoms (ʿĀlam al-Dharr), He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying], "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware" * Or [lest] you say, "It was only that our fathers associated [others with Allah] before, and we were [only] descendants after them. Then would You destroy us for what the falsifiers have done?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172-173].

The Qur'an has related their acknowledgment of following the fathers in more than one place in the Book of God, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed," they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers upon."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170], and He responds to them: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170].

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to them: you are lying in this claim. And if the matter were general, why did you not follow your father Adam, peace be upon him, who brought a method and walked in it? For had the people followed him, those after them would have imitated them, and so on, and God's method would have continued. Rather, desires have ruled you, and appetites have dominated you, so they took you out of your Lord's method and you opposed [Him]. Then is there not among you a rational man who understands this misguidance, and disdains to follow it, and seeks guidance?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verse 70:

Fa-hum ʿalā āthārihim (﴿So they are upon their traces﴾): meaning, they follow their path and imitate them. The word yuhraʿūna (﴿they are hastened﴾) means: they are driven and hurried, as if something were compelling them to hurry. This verb (yuhraʿūna) is in the passive voice, i.e., li-mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu (the form in which the doer is not named), as we say: zukima fulān (so-and-so was made to vomit/ill), where the agent is unknown.

Had the hastening in following the fathers been of their own choosing, it would have been said yahraʿūna with the fatḥa (active form). Rather it is yuhraʿūna, as if something were pushing them to imitate the fathers. God, glorified is He, thereby shows you that evil is more contagious (aʿdā), because there is no obligation (taklīf) on the soul in it and no restraint for desire; therefore a person runs toward it and hastens in seeking it.

As for guidance and the methodical path, a person does not hasten toward it, because it narrows for him the field of desires and restricts his movement within the frame of what God has legislated. So, in sum: they imitate the fathers while knowing that they are astray, in order to slip out from the bonds of the legal obligations.

Therefore, when God, exalted is He, took the covenant from us while we were in the world of the atoms (ʿālam al-dharr), He, glorified is He, said:

﴿And when your Lord brought forth from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying]: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." [This was] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this. Or [lest] you should say: 'Only our fathers associated partners [with God] before, and we were [their] descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?'"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172–173].

The Qur'an has recounted their acknowledgment of following the fathers in more than one place in the Book of God, He said, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," they say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ [al-Baqara: 170]. And He refutes them: ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ [al-Baqara: 170].

It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, is saying to them: you are lying in this claim. And if the matter were general, why did you not follow your father Adam, peace be upon him, who brought a method and walked upon it? If the people had followed him, those after them would have imitated them, and so on, and God's method would have continued. But rather, desires have governed you and passions have dominated you, so they took you out of your Lord's method and you opposed it. Then, is there not among you a rational man who comprehends this error, scorns to follow it, and seeks guidance?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verses 71–74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And certainly most of the former peoples had gone astray before them﴾ [al-Saffat: 71]. That is: these people are not unprecedented in going astray; many of those who came before them had gone astray. This means that a few believed, and the majority went astray. ﴿And certainly We sent among them warners﴾ [al-Saffat: 72]. That is: We did not leave them in their heedlessness; rather, We sent to them messengers to warn them and caution them.

We have said that within the human soul itself there are innate immune defenses, which protect its owner from disobedience and from error, even if he is alone, away from people. If this defense weakens in him and he opposes the method of God, the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), the repentant and returning soul (al-nafs al-awwabah), blames him, rebukes him until he repents and returns. If he becomes accustomed to disobedience and the self-reproaching soul grows weak in him, and he no longer has a deterrent from within himself, then society deters him: the society that enjoins good and forbids evil, the sincere society that establishes among its members the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿and they enjoin upon one another the truth, and they enjoin upon one another patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3].

There is a difference between: waṣṣū (they enjoined) and tawāṣaw (they enjoined upon one another). Tawāṣaw means: some of you advise others, so in it there is an interaction among the members of society; for society, even the believing and devout one, people vary within it in terms of uprightness and application of the method, and it is inevitable that in society there will be someone who weakens and goes astray, or is struck by heedlessness, so he finds someone who deters him, and finds someone who reminds him until he returns to the right path.

So when the deterrent is absent from society and corruption spreads throughout it, we say: heaven intervenes with a new messenger and a new method.

We know that the messenger comes as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. But here the Truth, Glorified is He, specified warning: ﴿And certainly We sent among them warners﴾ [al-Saffat: 72]. Why? They said: because repelling harm takes precedence over securing benefit. To clarify this matter, we said: if a person throws you an apple, for example, and another throws a stone at you, there is no doubt you will first push the stone away from yourself.

As for His saying: ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat: 73], that is: reflect on the outcome of warning. The messengers of God warned everyone, but did everyone benefit from the warning? No, rather some of them benefited from it, and some turned away from it. Therefore, the Truth, Glorified is He, after it brought this exception: ﴿except the chosen servants of God﴾ [al-Saffat: 74], that is: those whom He purified and chose for His worship and obedience, and they are the ones who benefited from the warning.

After the Truth, Glorified is He, had spoken of the procession of the messengers in summary, saying: ﴿And certainly We sent among them warners﴾ [al-Saffat: 72], He, Glorified is He, wished to speak about them with some detail, so He said, Glorified is He:

﴿And certainly Noah called out to Us, and how excellent were the Responders. And We delivered him and his family from the great distress...﴾.

It means: We did not leave them in their heedlessness; rather, We sent Messengers to them to warn them and caution them.

We have said that within the human soul itself there are self-immunities (manaʿat dhatiyya), which protect their owner from sin and from error, even if he is alone, away from people. If this immunity weakens in him and he opposes the method of God, the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwama, the soul that blames its owner), the one that turns back in repentance (al-awwaba), blames him, and keeps reproaching him until he repents and returns. If he becomes accustomed to sin and the self-reproaching soul grows weak in him, and he no longer has a restraint from his own self, then society restrains him: the society that enjoins good and forbids evil (al-amr bi'l-maʿruf wa'l-nahy ʿan al-munkar), the sincere society that establishes among its members the words of the Most High:

﴿And advise one another to truth, and advise one another to patience﴾ [al-ʿAsr: 3].

There is a difference between "waṣṣaw" and "tawāṣaw." Tawāṣaw means that some of you counsel others, so in it there is interaction among the members of society. This is because in society, even a believing and devout one, people vary in uprightness and in applying the method, and there must be among society those who weaken and deviate, or who are struck by heedlessness, so they find someone who restrains them and someone who reminds them until they return to the right path.

So when restraint is lost from society and corruption spreads throughout it, we say: the heavens have intervened with a new Messenger and a new method.

We know that the Messenger comes as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. But here the Most High singled out warning: "And We had certainly sent among them warners." Why? They said: because averting harm takes precedence over securing benefit. To clarify this matter, we said: if someone throws you an apple, for example, and another throws a stone at you, there is no doubt you will first push the stone away from yourself.

﴿And certainly Noah called out to Us, and how excellent were the Responders. And We delivered him and his family from the great distress...﴾.

But why did He begin with our master Noah (peace be upon him)? They said: Because his call was similar to the call of our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham and Moses and Jesus: that you establish the religion and do not become divided therein﴾ [ash-Shura: 13].

Allah the Exalted enjoined upon Noah, and enjoined upon others of the messengers who are higher than him, yet He joined them to him and placed him at the forefront. They said: Because Noah has a particularity in the environment in which he existed, and in those who believed in him. Those who believed in him were the ones who were saved in the Ark, and they alone were present in the whole world at that time. So it is as if he had a universality of message with respect to the subject, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has a universality of message, but in the universality of the subject.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us﴾ [as-Saffat: 75], the word (nadana, "called Us") indicates that he (peace be upon him) exhausted all his means in calling his people and they did not succeed. This is evident from his saying in another place, as the Qur'an relates: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except wicked disbelievers﴾ [Nuh: 26-27]. Noah only made this supplication against his people after despair from them, and after he found that the means of faith surrounding him from his followers were insufficient. So to whom does he resort? He resorts to Allah, for He alone is capable of delivering him from them. So he calls out: O my Lord, You sent me, so do not abandon me. This is a natural phenomenon for everyone who seeks help and calls for aid. When a danger befalls you and you cannot repel it by your own strength and cunning, you seek help from the nearest people to you; if you do not find [help], you seek it from the distant. If the helper is rare, you say, as we mentioned earlier, (ya huwa), meaning: O my Lord, there is none other than You who can aid me.

Then comes the response to this call: ﴿And how excellent were the Responders﴾ [as-Saffat: 75], because he (peace be upon him) was an excellent caller, so he must be met with excellent responders. He did not say "how excellent is the Responder," because the Truth answers him with His soldiers on earth, such as the air, the water, and the angels… ﴿And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. The result of this response: ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾ [as-Saffat: 76].

Here the orientalists stood and said: How could Allah have destroyed his son, is he not from his family? But in another place the Qur'an related to us the story of Noah (peace be upon him) and his son who deviated from him, so he drowned among those who were drowned, and Noah's pleas did not avail: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges﴾ [Hud: 45].

This confusion arises because people overlooked that the sonship of the prophets is not sonship by lineage, but sonship of faith in Allah. Therefore Allah responded to Noah: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous…﴾ [Hud: 46].

So the familyhood here is familyhood of creed and faith in Allah, not familyhood of blood and lineage. Therefore, if you consider this verse, you will find that the Exalted did not negate the person, but negated the person's action: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous…﴾ [Hud: 46].

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [text incomplete in the passage].

As for the words ﴿from the great distress﴾ [as-Saffat: 76], the intended meaning is the drowning. Distress (karb) is: the harm that you cannot repel from yourself, and that those around you cannot repel for you when you seek their help. If there is a means of escape for you in it, it is not called karb. The description of the distress here as "great" is because it came in such a way that no one could repel it. The water pours down from the sky, the earth gushes forth with it, and it covers the peaks of the mountains, so where is the escape then?

It is well known that water is the sustenance of the life of every living thing and one of the greatest blessings of Allah upon us. But if He, glorified be He, wills, He makes water a vengeance and a punishment. We have seen in the story of our master Moses (peace be upon him) how Allah saved Moses by water and destroyed Pharaoh by that very same water.

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [as-Saffat: 77], meaning: those who were with him in the Ark, who are the believers in his call. ﴿And We left upon him among the later generations﴾ [as-Saffat: 78], meaning: among people in general after him, praising him.

﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ [as-Saffat: 79].

So all people, upon hearing the biography of this prophet who bore the hardships in the cause of his call and remained in calling his people for that long lifespan, which is unlike people's lifespans, are obligated to send peace upon him, and when we hear his mention we should send peace upon him, saying: peace be upon him, ﴿Peace be upon Noah﴾ [as-Saffat: 79], meaning: grant him safety and peace. ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [as-Saffat: 80], meaning: this is a established practice of Allah concerning His prophets, that He grants them victory and preserves for them a good remembrance after them. ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾ [as-Saffat: 81].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 37, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat: 83]. That is: Abraham, peace be upon him, was of the shi'a (followers) of our master Noah. That is, among his adherents who followed him and walked in his method. The shi'a (shiyah, followers) are those who support a person in his thought, believing in it, and even try to carry his call to people along with him, and to bear harm in pursuit of that. From here the well-known sect that followed Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was named the Shi'a, and you certainly know the difference between the Shi'a (shi'a) and the Shuyu'iyya (communism).

But, why did the Truth, glory be to Him, begin the procession of the messengers here with Noah, peace be upon him, and then follow him with Abraham, peace be upon him?

He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. This is the reason, because soundness of heart is the foundation of religion and of creed, because the fitrah of Allah upon which He created people from the beginning is entirely built upon the form of righteousness and soundness; if corruption befalls this fitrah, it is from the human being.

Therefore, our master Abraham was praised for soundness of heart: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [al-Saffat: 84]. It is the heart upon which he was originally created, which remained as it was without change, so he lived with it, and his Lord received him with it in this world, and therefore he will attain it in the Hereafter: ﴿The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 88-89].

So the first soundness with which Allah created him he kept company with by keeping company with the method of Allah, so he was safe in this world, and he met Allah with a sound heart in the Hereafter. Thus Allah described His prophet Abraham in the best of descriptions.

And reflect on the phrase ﴿when he came to his Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 84], for it suggests that our master Abraham did not wait for a messenger to come to him calling him; rather he turned to Allah himself, and came with his thought, seeking and contemplating the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, until he was guided to Allah.

Therefore, when Allah, may He be exalted, wished to introduce His prophet Abraham and present him to the assembly of faith, He spoke this concise telegram: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, a hanif﴾ [al-Nahl: 120].

You know that the Truth, glory be to Him, created talents and distributed them among people, so each of us has a talent in something, so that people remain interdependent in need: you need me and I need you. As for our master Abraham, he gathered and possessed all the talents that are in a whole nation. So the meaning of ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾ [al-Nahl: 120] is that he possessed the talents of a nation.

Therefore, peace be upon him, he deserved that Allah show him the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth. People in general are content with the world of dominion (mulk), but he went beyond this world to the world of malakut. Why? Because he stripped himself of any trace of certainty in anyone other than Allah, as is evident when he was thrown into the fire and the angel came to him offering help: "Do you have any need?" And our master Abraham, with the store of faith and certainty in Allah he possessed, said: "As for you, no." He said this at this grievous time and this overwhelming distress.

And His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 85]. This is counted among soundness of heart, because he loved something and found happiness in it, so he wanted to transmit it to others, and first among them relatives, for they are the people most worthy that your goodness reach them. Therefore, the first thing Abraham did was call his father and his people: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 85].

The word (li-abihi, "to his father") occurs in the Qur'an ten times, only one of which is for our master Joseph, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me"﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. The remaining nine are for our master Abraham, beginning with Surah al-An'am through Surah al-Mumtahana. Of these nine, there is one place where he combined the proper name and the descriptive term, saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error"﴾ [al-An'am: 74].

In the remaining eight, the word (li-abihi) came without mention of Azar, as though the name Azar came in this place to make us aware of something: that when you combine a descriptive term with a proper name, the descriptive term must be shared with someone other than the named person. We gave an example for that, saying: if you want to ask about a person, and his son meets you in the street, you say to him: "Is your father present?"

Because this question is directed only to his real father. But if you say: "Is your father Muhammad present?", you undoubtedly mean his uncle, because you distinguished him by name to remove the commonality of fatherhood.

So then: Azar was not the real father of our master Abraham; rather he was his uncle, and there is no strangeness in that, for the Qur'an calls an uncle a father in His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac, one God, and to Him we are Muslims"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133].

It is known that Ishmael was the brother of Isaac, yet He included him among the fathers in relation to our master Jacob, peace be upon them all.

And our master Abraham, in the context of calling his father and people, asks them this question: ﴿What do you worship?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 70], and in another place: ﴿What do you worship?﴾ [al-Saffat: 85], and ﴿What are these statues to which you are devoted?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 52].

Here: ﴿What do you worship? * Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire?﴾ [al-Saffat: 85-86]. All of these are rhetorical questions of denunciation. We said that a question is stronger than a statement, because a statement can be denied, whereas a question makes the opponent acknowledge the matter and he cannot deny it.

Ifk (falsehood) is the most abominable kind of lying, because abomination in lying comes in stages. How? They said: we look at the subject in which the lie occurs. If it concerns the supreme reality, namely the divine essence, it is the most abominable lie, like one who claims a partner for Allah.

If the lie is against human beings, it depends on the one against whom one lies. For example, those who accused our lady Aisha and engaged in slandering her honor, Allah called it ifk (ifk) because of its enormity and the great station of the one against whom this lie was told. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, those who came up with the falsehood are a group among you...﴾ [al-Nur: 11].

Among the meanings of ifk is overturning a thing from its proper form, and reversing the reality, and of this is His saying: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ [al-Najm: 53].

The meaning is: do you desire gods of falsehood and lies besides Allah? ﴿So what is your thought about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat: 87]. Tell us, what do you think of Allah? And what in His divinity do you dislike, glory be to Him? And how do you deceive yourselves, so that you turn away from Him, glory be to Him, while He is the Lord of the worlds? An example of this is His saying: ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6].

Therefore one of the knowers said: It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, taught people the answer: "What deceived me about Allah is that He is generous." The anecdote here is that a man saw another performing prayer hastily, pecking at it, and he said to him: "By Allah, if you owed five piastres to someone, would it be right to give it to him with a rubbed-off coin?" The man said: "By Allah, if he were generous he would accept it without examining it."

So it is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, marvels at those who associated partners with Him, despite the clarity of the proof of the invalidity of their shirk. A thing is only marvelled at when it comes contrary to what it ought to be in truthfulness; therefore He, glory be to Him, said at the beginning of al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life, then to Him you will be returned?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28].

That is: this is an amazing matter from you, and a matter the intellect does not accept.

Then our master Abraham, peace be upon him, began to fulfill the saying of his Lord: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the malakut of the heavens and the earth...﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. It has already been noted that we distinguished between al-mulk, al-mulk and al-malakut.

Almighty Allah says: "When he came to his Lord with a sound heart." This is the reason: soundness of heart is the foundation of religion and of creed, because the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people from the beginning is entirely built upon the form of righteousness and soundness. If corruption befalls this fitrah, it comes from the human being.

For this reason, Allah praised our master Ibrahim (Abraham) with soundness of heart: "When he came to his Lord with a sound heart." This is the heart upon which he was created at first, and it remained as it was, unchanged. He lived by it, and he came to his Lord with it in this world; therefore he attains it in the Hereafter: ﴿On the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:88-89].

Reflect on the phrase "When he came to his Lord," for it suggests that our master Ibrahim did not wait for a messenger to come to him calling him; rather, he turned to Allah himself, and came with his thought, seeking and contemplating the dominion of the heavens and the earth, until he was guided to Allah.

His words, glory be to Him: "When he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'" This is counted among the soundness of the heart, because he loved something and was made happy by it, so he wanted to transfer it to others, and the first of them were his relatives, for they are the people most entitled to have your goodness extended to them. Therefore, the first thing Ibrahim (Abraham) did was call his father and his people: "When he said to his father and his people, 'What is it that you worship?'"
The meaning: Do you want gods, falsehood (ifkan, إفكاً) and lies, besides Allah?

﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾

Tell us: what do you think of God? What is it about His divinity that displeases you? And how do you deceive yourselves, turning away from Him, when He is the Lord of the worlds...

So the Truth, glory be to Him, is astonished at those who ascribe partners to Him, even though the proof that their polytheism is false is clear. And a thing is only regarded as astonishing when it comes in a way other than what truth requires it to be...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verses 88–96:

The Exalted said about our master Ibrahim (Abraham), ﴿So he cast a glance at the stars﴾ [al-Saffat: 88]. This was Ibrahim's first step into the realm of the dominion (malakut). The "glance" (nazra) here is not a hasty, passing look, but a searching, deliberate, patient contemplation. It carries the sense of "saw with careful reflection and inference," as in our saying: "this is a matter that requires consideration" (fiha nazar), meaning reflection and deliberation. The plural of najm (star) is nujum, and a najm is anything that shines in the sky with its own light, not by reflecting the light of the sun. Accordingly, the sun is also one of the stars.

So the Exalted's words ﴿he cast a glance at the stars﴾ [al-Saffat: 88] indicate that it was a long, reflective, comprehensive look, since it took in a planet, a moon and a sun. For this reason, Allah explained this glance in another place, saying: ﴿And thus We showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain (in faith). So when the night covered him over, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set." Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray." Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate with Allah. Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining (to truth), and I am not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 75–79].

Thus Ibrahim's glance was long and deliberate, for it spanned the whole of the rising and setting of the planet, then the rising and setting of the moon, then the rising and setting of the sun. When he (peace be upon him) saw that these apparitions were not fit to be gods worshipped, he said: ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾ [al-Saffat: 89]. Some regard this as one of the "lies" of our master Ibrahim, that he told his people he was sick.

However, some understood "saqam" (sickness) as sickness of the bodies, whereas what is meant here is sickness of the heart, and his preoccupation with what a person cannot bear: the people's denial of the matter of divinity. This is a matter that wearies him and keeps him awake.

This is the sickness that our master Ibrahim meant: ﴿So he said, "Indeed, I am ill"﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], that is, weary in thought from people's denial of the matter of divinity. Thus Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was not looking at the stars to find evidence that he himself would be convinced by, but was seeking a material sign in the universe that he could convey to the people.

But what made him tell the people, "I am ill"? They said: because they used to gather on a day of festival, so he said, "I am ill" so that he would not go out with them, and so that he would be free for what he had resolved upon, the smashing of the idols. The Exalted says: ﴿So they turned their backs and departed﴾ [al-Saffat: 90], that is, they went away and left him.

﴿Then he slipped away to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 91]. The word "raagha" means to go off secretly, so that no one sees him, or to slip away like someone who wishes to leave a gathering without them noticing: he walks two steps, then stops, then walks on, then hides behind something, and so on until he is out. This meaning we express in colloquial speech as: "so-and-so zawwagh" or "zaagh."

Our master Ibrahim did this and slipped away to their gods to smash them, but before smashing them he mocked them. ﴿He said﴾ [al-Saffat: 91], that is, to the gods, ﴿"Will you not eat?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 91]. When they did not answer, he said: ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 92]. He said this in scorn and mockery of them.

After that he turned upon them, striking them: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ [al-Saffat: 93]. We have said that "al-yamin" (the right hand/side) denotes the side of strength, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿They said, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right"﴾ [al-Saffat: 28], that is, from the side of strength and domination. The meaning is that our master Ibrahim began to smash them with force and break them, until the breaking made a loud sound that the people heard. ﴿So they came rushing toward him﴾ [al-Saffat: 94], that is, hastening.

When he saw them, ﴿he said, "Do you worship what you carve? And Allah created you and what you make"﴾ [al-Saffat: 95–96]. The interrogation here is for astonishment and denunciation. He says to them: how can you worship a god made by your own hands, which you carve from stone? You are the people most knowledgeable about it: you see it fall, you set it up in its place, it breaks and you repair it, the flood sweeps it away and rolls it in the mud, and you pull it out.

So how can such a god be worshipped? How can you turn toward its worship and leave the worship of Allah, the true God, who created you and what you do?

Of course they had no answer to this question, and they had no reply to Ibrahim except the reply of force and brutality. They had no argument and no logic with which to defend their gods:

﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and cast him into the blaze." So they intended a scheme against him...﴾

Thus Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was not looking at the stars to find evidence that he himself would be convinced by, but was seeking a material sign in the universe that he could convey to the people.

But what made him tell the people, "I am ill"? They said: because they used to gather on a day of festival, so he said, "I am ill" so that he would not go out with them, and so that he would be free for what he had resolved upon, the smashing of the idols. The Exalted says: ﴿So they turned their backs and departed﴾ [al-Saffat: 90], that is, they went away and left him.

﴿Then he slipped away to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 91]. The word "raagha" means to go off secretly, so that no one sees him, or to slip away like someone who wishes to leave a gathering without them noticing: he walks two steps, then stops, then walks on, then hides behind something, and so on until he is out. This meaning we express in colloquial speech as: "so-and-so zawwagh" or "zaagh."

Our master Ibrahim did this and slipped away to their gods to smash them, but before smashing them he mocked them. ﴿He said﴾ [al-Saffat: 91], that is, to the gods, ﴿"Will you not eat?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 91]. When they did not answer, he said: ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 92]. He said this in scorn and mockery of them.

After that he turned upon them, striking them: ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ [al-Saffat: 93]. We have said that "al-yamin" (the right hand/side) denotes the side of strength, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿They said, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right"﴾ [al-Saffat: 28], that is, from the side of strength and domination. The meaning is that our master Ibrahim began to smash them with force and break them, until the breaking made a loud sound that the people heard. ﴿So they came rushing toward him﴾ [al-Saffat: 94], that is, hastening.

When he saw them, ﴿he said, "Do you worship what you carve? And Allah created you and what you make"﴾ [al-Saffat: 95–96]. The interrogation here is for astonishment and denunciation. He says to them: how can you worship a god made by your own hands, which you carve from stone? You are the people most knowledgeable about it: you see it fall, you set it up in its place, it breaks and you repair it, the flood sweeps it away and rolls it in the mud, and you pull it out.

So how can such a god be worshipped? How can you turn toward its worship and leave the worship of Allah, the true God, who created you and what you do?

Of course they had no answer to this question, and they had no reply to Ibrahim except the reply of force and brutality. They had no argument and no logic with which to defend their gods:

﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and cast him into the blaze." So they intended a scheme against him...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verses 97–98:

You know the story of the fire that they kindled, then they threw the Prophet of God, Ibrahim (Abraham), into the middle of it. This is the scheme (kayd) that they intended against Ibrahim. God, exalted is He, would not send a prophet and then abandon him, so God turned their scheme back upon them: ﴿Indeed, they are scheming a scheme. And I am scheming a scheme﴾ [al-Tariq: 15-16].

The meaning of ﴿So We made them the lowest﴾ [al-Saffat: 98] means: in this position, and in this situation which they brought about against Ibrahim. They were not "the lowest" because they were disbelievers; rather, they were "the lowest" (asfalin) because they exalted themselves over Ibrahim and gained power over him, and they were able to throw him into the fire while it was blazing, and at that moment they thought they were the dominant ones.

But quickly the reality of the situation was revealed, and the great sign that God, exalted is He, intended appeared. For if God had willed, Ibrahim would have been saved, so they could not seize hold of him. And if He, glorified is He, had willed, the sky would have rained upon the fire and extinguished it. But God willed to nullify their proofs: if Ibrahim had escaped from their hands, they would have said, "If he had not escaped, we would have burned him"; and if the sky had rained, they would have said, "It is a natural phenomenon with which we have no connection."

But here is Ibrahim, and here is the fire blazing, and yet Ibrahim is saved after the call of truth and the word of truth came to creation: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69].

The address is from God, exalted is He, and the command is to the fire according to its nature and with its own attributes: ﴿Be coolness and safety﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69], not in its essence, but ﴿upon Ibrahim﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69]. This is a particular distinction of this very fire: outwardly it is blazing, but in its reality it is ﴿coolness and safety﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69] upon Ibrahim. It is like the tree of zaqqum: it appears to them as a green tree, yet it is a fire that burns them.

Thus God made them, in this position, ﴿the lowest﴾ [al-Saffat: 98], that is, within the scheme they had devised. They scheme, and God schemes, and a scheme must be judged by the one who executes it.

When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) found no benefit in calling his people, he said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ The meaning is: going to support His religion; otherwise, his Lord is present with him and everywhere. Or [it means]: emigrating to my Lord, i.e., to another place, where I will find someone who hears me and responds to my call. And as long as I am going to my Lord, ﴿He will guide me﴾, i.e., He will guide me to the good station suited to my call.

Then Abraham prayed to his Lord: "My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous" [al-Saffat: 100]. That is, grant me a righteous, believing offspring. When the prophet of God wishes for offspring, he does not wish for them to be a remembrance, a source of support, or an extension through which an inheritance passes on. Rather, prophets desire a son to carry their message and to be a model of faith who inherits their call. For this reason, in the story of our master Zechariah, He says: "who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub; and make him, my Lord, one well-pleasing" [Maryam: 6].

It was as if our master Abraham found it grievous that his lifespan would not be extended so that he could be a soldier in the ranks of God's method on earth. So he said: "O Lord, comfort my eye by letting me see a son of mine who bears the responsibility of prophethood after me."

He said "My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous" [al-Saffat: 100] and did not say "My Lord, grant me the righteous." He thus wanted from his offspring someone who is righteous within the broader righteousness of others. He desired righteousness for his descendants and for others as well. Therefore his Lord answered him: "So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy" [al-Saffat: 101]. Al-Halim (the forbearing) is the one whom anger does not provoke, and who bears matters to the extent that his character is at ease. Among forbearance is leaving off disputation and obstinacy, even when one is in the right.

For this reason, a hadith of our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), states: "I guarantee a house in the outskirts of Paradise for one who abandons disputation, even if he is in the right..."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 101:

﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy.﴾ Glad tidings (bushra) about a thing come before its existence. God described him as one who would be forbearing while he was still a boy. That is to say, he would combine the two attributes together, because forbearance (ḥilm) usually forms in a man who is mature and able to weigh matters. The distinguishing feature here is that the boy is characterized by forbearance in his youth.

Indeed, the boy's forbearance appeared in the first test he faced, when his father said to him:

﴿O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so consider what you think.﴾ Reflect on what the boy said, while his father was about to slaughter him:

﴿He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast.﴾ This is forbearance, manifest in him while he was still a boy.

I'll translate this passage faithfully. Note that the Qur'anic verses in the passage are rendered by their meaning, inside ﴿ ﴾ markers as required.

Here, the context did not address the pregnancy of Lady Hajar nor her giving birth to Isma'il. Rather, it moved directly from the good news of him to the stage of his reaching the age of striving (al-sa'y) alongside his father. Then He, glorified is He, said after it: ﴿And when he reached with him the age of striving﴾, because it is the Truth, glorified is He, who speaks, and who narrates.

From the eloquence (balaghah) is that what is known from the context is omitted, and this is one of the characteristics of the Qur'anic style. In the story of Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him) and the hoopoe (hudhhud), Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Go with this letter of mine, then throw it to them, then turn away from them and see what they return⦆ [al-Naml: 28]. Then the context abridges many events and says:

﴿She said: "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter"﴾ [al-Naml: 29], and it did not address the journey of the hoopoe, nor how the message was delivered to the queen.

Likewise here: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾ * ﴿And when he reached with him the age of striving﴾. His reaching the age of striving indicates that the good news was fulfilled, the boy was born, and he reached the age of striving with his father. There is a difference between (reaching the age of striving) in general, and (reaching the age of striving with his father), because a boy is not assigned work except according to his capacity for movement, and according to his health and endurance. Isma'il at this time reached the age of striving with his father only, because his compassionate father would not assign him except what he is able to do of tasks and life affairs; so the boy does what he is able to do and leaves what he cannot do to his father. Had he been with another person, perhaps he would have assigned him what he could not bear.

So when the boy reached this stage, he said: ﴿O my dear son, indeed I see in the dream that I am slaughtering you﴾. The meaning: I see in the dream that it is required of me that I slaughter you, not that the slaughter was accomplished in the dream; the matter ended, as evidenced by Isma'il's reply: ﴿He said: "O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast"﴾.

Consider here forbearance in its reality, and the greatness of the response in this difficult trial. ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded﴾, and he did not say: "Do what you wish", because his obedience to his father here stems from his inner obedience to Allah and his compliance with the command of his Lord. He fully realizes that his father is receiving the command from Allah, even if this command came in the form of a vision. Thus, despite his youth, he knows that the visions of the prophets are true revelation (wahy haqq).

And Prophet Ibrahim calls his son "Ya bunayya" in this diminutive form, because "bunayy" is the diminutive of "ibn" (son); he did not say "ya ibni". The paternal tenderness bound him, and he presented this trial to him while he was full of the emotion of love for his son and compassion for him, because he was still young. It is known that a father's tenderness is in proportion to the child's need; therefore, when an Arab woman was asked: "Which of your sons is dearest to you?" she said: "The sick until he recovers, the absent until he returns, and the young until he grows up."

So his saying "ya bunayya" means: I do not treat you as an equal, but as a young one in need of paternal tenderness; so receive my commands accompanied by this paternal and heartfelt emotion.

And his saying: ﴿fa-unzur﴾ (so consider) means: think and reflect, ﴿what do you see﴾, i.e., in this vision. It is as if the young one in this matter is required to do two things: to be dutiful to his father, and to be dutiful to the Lord of his father. ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded﴾: his saying "do" is dutifulness to his father, and his saying "what you are commanded" is dutifulness to his father's Lord.

Then Prophet Isma'il, despite his youth, affirms his understanding of this matter and his awareness of this trial, and says: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast﴾, i.e., in the face of this affliction.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verse 103:

﴿So when they had both submitted﴾ meaning: both of them together submitted to the command of God, yielded to His judgment, and each surrendered the direction of his movement in the act to his Lord. Ibrahim resolved to slaughter, and Isma'il complied, and said to his father: ﴿You will find me, God willing, of the steadfast.﴾

The trial concerning our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a compound trial this time. He had been tested in his youth when he was thrown into the fire, and he succeeded in the trial. But this time the trial came when he was an old man; a son was given to him in old age, so he was dearer to him than his own self, and he was commanded to slay him.

Ibrahim could have slaughtered him unawares, without informing him of this matter of slaughter, but he wanted to make him a partner with him in the reward, and that his heart should not be embittered against him, since he was slaughtering him without a reason.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿and He had flung him down upon his brow﴾ meaning: he threw him onto his face, or onto his side. They said: that happened by the counsel of the son, so that his father would not see his face at the moment of slaughter, lest compassion for him seize him and he would not slaughter. It is as if the son was helping his father and assisting him in completing the matter. Thus submission appeared clearly: the son was laid on the ground, and the father had the knife in his hand, actually trying to slaughter his son. And what a son! His only son, who was granted to him at...

The trial is not that the son should die; rather it is that his father should slaughter him with his own hand, not through another person, and slaughter him on the basis of a vision rather than a clear command. Therefore we said it is a compound trial, because its aspects of testing are many. Ibrahim and his son passed this trial successfully, and he, peace be upon him, merited that God say concerning him: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community﴾ [al-Nahl: 120].

Meaning: "Lower your hand, O Ibrahim, from slaughtering your only son." Indeed, this was nothing but a clear trial (balaʼ mubin), meaning evident and severe for you and your son. It is called "clear" (mubin) because it makes evident the strength of the faith of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in receiving the command from Allah, even though it was difficult and harsh, and then in submitting to it and obeying. Likewise, the trial was also for his son, who submitted and complied.

It is clear because it makes manifest the strength of Ibrahim's faith, peace be upon him, in receiving the command from Allah, even though it was difficult and harsh, and then submitting to it and obeying. Likewise the trial was for his son, who submitted and complied.

Then came the ransom: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107]. "Dhibh" here means "madhbuh" (that which is slaughtered), and it is the ram that Allah sent down as a ransom for Isma'il.

His saying ﴿"then see what you think"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102] means: reflect and ponder ﴿what you see﴾ [al-Saffat: 102], that is, in this vision. It is as if the young one in this matter is required to do two things: be dutiful to his Lord and dutiful to his father. ﴿He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]: his saying ﴿do﴾ is dutifulness toward his father, and his saying ﴿as you are commanded﴾ is dutifulness toward his father's Lord.

Then Sayyidina Isma'il, despite his youth, affirms his understanding of this matter and his awareness of this trial, saying: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast﴾ [al-Saffat: 102], that is, under this affliction. ﴿So when they both submitted﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning: both of them together submitted to the command of Allah and yielded to His judgment, and each of them surrendered the reins of his movement in action to his Lord. Ibrahim resolved to slaughter, and Isma'il complied and said to his father, ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast﴾ [al-Saffat: 102].

The trial for Sayyidina Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a compound trial this time. He had been tested in his youth when he was thrown into the fire, and he succeeded in that trial. This time, however, the trial came when he was an old man, to whom a son was born in his old age. This son was dearer to him than himself, and he is commanded to kill him.

Ibrahim could have slaughtered him unawares, without informing him of this slaughter, but he wanted to make him a partner in the reward, and that his heart should not be aggrieved against him while he slaughtered him without cause.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And he put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning: he laid him on his face or on his side. It is said that this was by the advice of the son, so that his father would not see his face at the moment of slaughter, lest compassion for him seize him and he not slaughter. It is as if the son was helping his father and assisting him in completing the matter. Thus submission appeared clearly: the son was laid on the ground, and the father had the knife in his hand, actually trying to slaughter his son, and what a son! His only son, whom he was granted in old age.

The trial was not that the son should die, but that his father should slaughter him with his own hand, not through another person, and slaughter him on the basis of a vision, not an explicit command. Therefore we said it is a compound trial, because its aspects are many. Ibrahim and his son passed this trial successfully, and peace be upon him deserved that Allah say about him: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾ [al-Nahl: 120].

We say: when Ibrahim and his son reached this degree of submission to Allah, Allah called to him: ﴿And We called to him, "O Ibrahim"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104]. It is as if Allah was with them both, watching this submission from two servants who were truthful with Allah, so the relief of Allah came to them: ﴿And We called to him, "O Ibrahim * You have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers * Indeed, this was the clear trial"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104-106].

The meaning: lift your hand, O Ibrahim, from slaughtering your only son, for the matter was only a clear trial, that is, evidently severe for you and your son. It is clear because it makes manifest the strength of Ibrahim's faith, peace be upon him, in receiving the command from Allah, even though it was difficult and harsh, and then submitting to it and obeying. Likewise the trial was for his son, who submitted and complied.

Then came the ransom: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107]. "Dhibh" here means "madhbuh" (that which is slaughtered), and it is the ram that Allah sent down as a ransom for Isma'il.

The Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verses 105–107:

Here the context does not address the pregnancy of Sayyidah Hajar nor her giving birth to Isma'il. Rather, it moves directly from the good news of him to the stage of his reaching the age of striving (al-sa'y) alongside his father. After that, the Exalted says: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of striving﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. That is because the Truth, glory be to Him, is the one who speaks, and He is the one who relates.

Part of the eloquence is to omit what is known from the context, and this is one of the characteristics of the Qur'anic style. In the story of Sayyidina Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the hoopoe (al-hudhud), the Exalted says: ﴿Go with this letter of mine and drop it to them, then turn away from them and see what they will return﴾ [al-Naml: 28]. Then the context abridges many events and says: ﴿She said, "O chiefs, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter"﴾ [al-Naml: 29]. It does not dwell on the hoopoe's journey, nor on how the message reached the queen.

Likewise here: ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy * And when he reached with him the age of striving﴾ [al-Saffat: 101-102]. His reaching the age of striving indicates that the good tidings were fulfilled, the boy was born, and he reached the age of striving alongside his father. There is a difference between (reached the striving) in general and (reached with his father the striving), because a boy is not assigned work except according to his capacity for movement, his health, and his endurance. Isma'il at this time reached the striving only alongside his father, because his tender father would not assign him except what he is able to do of the affairs and tasks of life. The boy does what he is able to do and leaves to his father what he cannot do; and had he been with another person, that person might have assigned him what he could not bear.

So when the boy reached this stage, ﴿he said, "O my dear son, indeed I see in a dream that I sacrifice you"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. The meaning: I see in a dream that it is required of me that I slaughter you, not that the slaughter took place in the dream. The matter ended by the evidence of Isma'il's reply: ﴿He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102].

Consider here the forbearance in its reality, and the greatness of the response in this difficult trial: ﴿"O my father, do as you are commanded"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. He did not say, "Do what you wish," because his obedience to his father here derives from his inner obedience to Allah and his compliance with the command of his Lord. He fully realises that his father receives the command from Allah, even if this command came in the form of a vision. Thus, despite his youth, he knows that the visions of the prophets are true revelation.

Sayyidina Ibrahim calls his son ﴿"O my dear son"﴾ [al-Saffat: 102] in the diminutive, for bunayya is the diminutive of ibn (son), and he did not say "O my son." The paternal tenderness had bound him, and he presented this trial to him while filled with the emotion of love for his son and compassion for him, because he was still young. It is known that a father's tenderness is in proportion to the child's need.
