So: He called them and took them away from business and work, which is the summit of the movement of life, namely trading (bay'). Although trading is linked to buying (shira'), trading is stronger, so He singled it out for mention and did not say "leave off trading and buying." Why? They said: because He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of human nature, and He knows that man is reluctant when it comes to buying, not keen on it, but he is keen on selling and strives for it. So when the people of the house ask you to buy something, you may procrastinate in buying it or postpone it, and you are pleased when you go and find the shop closed. But if you were a seller, you would be most eager to sell. Why? Because the buyer spends and the seller receives. So the Mighty and Majestic mentioned trading because it is the fruit of the movement.

After the prayer ends, He said: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse through the land and seek of Allah's bounty...﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. So: taking you to prayer is a form of work, and He returned you after the prayer to work and striving.

When you reflect on the wording of the hadith (prophetic saying): i.e., these five are the pillars upon which Islam stands, and the building is other than the foundation it is built upon. Is the building we live in made only of the foundation and the columns? So: Islam is not the five pillars; rather Islam is broader than that. The pillars are the charge (shuhna) to which your Lord summons you, so you take from meeting Him the support that helps you carry out the movement of life.

We illustrate this with the battery: when you take it to be charged, we do not benefit from it during the charging period; rather, we give it the charge it needs so that it can work afterward.

Among the wonders of divine mercy is that God made going to the charge of human energy an obligatory duty that you must perform. You must meet Me five times a day and night, because you are My creation and My handiwork, and the maker knows best what repairs his handiwork. Imagine a piece of workmanship presented to its maker five times a day and night: would any defect remain in it? This is the case with a maker who is a human; how much more so with the Maker who is the Lord of mankind and their Creator, glory be to Him.

A human maker repairs his handiwork with a material thing, such as a nail or a spare part, for example. But the Creator, glory be to Him, repairs you without any material thing, because the engineer and his handiwork are material, so he repairs with material. But the Creator, glory be to Him, is the unseen (ghayb). So when He repairs a defect in you, He repairs it through the unseen, so you neither feel it nor see it.

So: we say that one must understand religion as it truly is, and understand that each of us has a task. If someone else excels over you, know that his excellence is for your benefit and returns to you, because through his excellence he provides a service to you, while he does not benefit from you. Whoever is skilled at a craft certainly benefits himself and benefits others, unlike the one who is skilled at nothing.

That is why we say among the peasants: "the carpenter's door is off its hinges" (bab al-najjar mukhala'). The carpenter's skill appears when he makes things for others, because he receives a wage; but he does not practise his craft for himself. So: when you see one who excels over you, do not envy him or bear him a grudge; rather, wish him more, and wish him good. Something of this good will certainly reach you, and this excellence will return to you in the form of a service he provides for you.

That is why, when we were peasants, if one of us lost a cow or a buffalo, everyone would grieve, to the extent that once we saw a group weeping over a calf that had died, and we were surprised. People weep over a dead person among them, but over an animal?! Afterwards we came to know that this calf was the one that turns the water-wheel (saqiya) and ploughs the land from which these people eat, and the good of this land reaches them. In the countryside we did not buy cucumbers, molokhia, okra, and much else; rather, it was given as a gift and was not sold.

So: the gift extended among creatures returns to all creatures. When you see someone who excels, bless him, and when you see someone who is skilled at work that you are not skilled at, do not bear him a grudge, because you will need him to do your work well, even if you dislike him or are at odds with him. You are keen on him to work for you, because you know how skilled he is at the work, so you go to him out of concern for your own interest. In this way the required balance in society is achieved, and the affairs of creatures are set right on a foundation of need.

If you reflect on yourself, as God said: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21], you will find in yourself this balance between the organs. For example, you have the right hand, with which you perform certain tasks that suit it, and the left hand, with which you perform other tasks that suit it. The right hand is for noble, honored tasks, while the left is for what is less than that. The right is usually stronger than the left, more active, and more precise in handling.

Consider, for example, when you want to trim your nails: you trim the left hand with the right, and the cutting comes out precise and comfortable, unlike cutting the right with the left. So: the right hand's ability benefits the left, and the left's lack of ability benefits the right. This draws our attention to the fact that perfections in the universe are perfections that spread through it, like the spreading of water.

When God, glory be to Him, created the human vicegerent, He gave him formations suited to his task. The first of these formations are the organs that we call the senses, through which we perceive things, which they call the five outward senses. Their saying "outward" is a precaution against senses that will be discovered and that science knows; indeed, other senses beyond the five have been discovered in humans, such as the sense by which I know hunger, the sense of distance (hassat al-bayn) by which I distinguish the distance between two things, and the sense of muscle (hassat al-adala) by which I know the weight of things.

When you reflect on these five known senses, you find that the legal obligation (taklif shar'i) came in accordance with this formation of the senses. Each sense in a human has a function, and each organ has a task. The performance by each organ of its task is called "action" ('amal). The heart acts through intention, the tongue speaks, the ear hears, the nose smells, the hand touches things, and the eye sees. All of this is action.

Here we must distinguish between 'amal (action) and fi'l (deed), and deed is opposed by speech (qawl), which is the task of the tongue. So God said: ﴿O you who believe! Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2].

So: speech, which is the task of the tongue, took one part alone, and the rest of the senses took the other part. Speech belongs to the tongue, and deeds belong to the remaining senses. Why did the tongue take one share and the remaining senses the other? They said: because speech is the means of conveying from us what the messengers require, so that we may do it, and of conveying our requests from others so that they may do them.

So: all deeds are in the service of speech, and God's method does not come to us except through speech, which carries the command to the senses so that they act. And action is not necessarily physical labour; it may be inward action, such as the action of the heart, which is intention, as we have said. The Shari'a (sacred law) governs these senses and defines for them the framework within which they act, in light of what is permitted (halal) and forbidden (haram).

The task of the senses is to pick up perceptions and then present them to the intellect, which refines them with true refinement, by comparing them and knowing that this suits such-and-such and that suits such-and-such. After this refinement, it hands them over to the heart so that they become a belief (aqida) in it. The word 'aqida means a thing that is tied and cannot be untied, and is not presented for debate again in the intellect. For example, a small child is attracted by the beautiful shape of fire, so he tries to grasp it, and the fire burns him, and for the first time he feels heat. So a belief or intellectual principle forms in him that fire burns, and he does not approach it afterwards, and he continues all his life following this belief or this principle, without needing to test it again.

When this belief settles in the heart, the heart pumps it with the blood, so it travels through the whole body and permeates all the organs, and they absorb it. This explains for us the noble hadith... Then, after God, glory be to Him, gave man the organs and senses, He created the instincts (ghara'iz), which are matters necessary for you, fixed in your make-up, and you cannot dispense with them. But this instinct may press upon you and take you away from its purpose, and then the Shari'a must intervene to restrain its excess and return it to the balance for which God created it.

The Shari'a intervenes to elevate the instinct and refine it, not to suppress it and eliminate it. Eating is an instinct for preserving life, and what our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said suffices concerning it: "...and it should not go beyond that and turn into gluttony and excess." Curiosity is an instinct that God made for exploring His secrets in the universe and reflecting on His creatures. If it goes beyond this framework and becomes spying and tracking people's private faults, it has strayed from its task, and here the Shari'a intervenes to elevate it and return it to its balance.

The most fierce of human instincts is the sexual instinct, especially in youth. God made this instinct for preserving the species and continuing offspring. This is the task for which the sexual instinct was created, and the Shari'a has been keen to preserve this instinct accompanied by a method of its movement for those who created it, so that affairs may be set right, because offspring is the first wealth that must be preserved, so that the offspring may come noble and pure.

We have previously distinguished between legitimate offspring, attributed to the two parents, and illegitimate offspring, and how the former is met with joy, tenderness, compassion, and care, while the latter is met with hatred and unwillingness, and perhaps its mother thinks of getting rid of it, even by throwing it onto the street.

From here, religion has been keen to build the family on a sound foundation, with honour, dignity, and self-respect, under the shade of God's word and His method, which secures for you the safety of your lineage, so that it comes trustworthy, something you can rely on, which you care for, and which you raise in the best way. This is the aim of the Shari'a.

We have previously spoken about the difference between the lawful and the unlawful in this matter, and mentioned the noble hadith... So: this instinct is created in human nature for performing a task, and so that it remains within the framework for which it was created. But the reality is that many people take it out of its purpose. It is strange that a person should wrong the animal in this matter, when he says: "This is animal lust," and boasts of it.

This statement shows a lack of understanding of the animal's instinct, because the animal stops at the limits of its instinct as God created it. That is why we have never seen a female animal that conceived and then allowed a male to mount her afterwards. Likewise, the male sniffs her, knows that she is pregnant, and turns away from her.

Is this animal lust in the sense that we mean by this word? No, rather it is human... You may compare this instinct in the animal and in the human, and you will see the wonder of humans' departure from its intended purpose.

Among the wisdom of the Creator, glory be to Him, is that He linked the sexual instinct and offspring with enjoyment. This is because offspring has demands, consequences, and responsibilities. If there were no pleasure to encourage the human, he would shun the matter and turn away from it.

The Almighty, glory be to Him, deals with the believers according to one method, with contrasting matters such as honour and humiliation. The believer is not disposed to constant honour nor to constant humiliation; rather, the situation he lives in dictates to him whether he should be honourable or humble. So humility and submission are for his fellow believers, and honour and haughtiness are towards the disbelieving deniers, as God said describing our master, the Messenger of Allah, and the believers: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; and those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves...﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

So: they are firm and merciful at the same time, and this is evidence that the believer is not governed by his instincts except according to the measures of the Creator of instincts.

Also among the formations in the creation of man, after the senses and instincts, is that God created in man emotion (ʿatifa), and emotion is a feeling whose cause we do not know. That is why you meet a person and feel at ease with him, and another whom you dislike, just like that, without any prior dealing. Why then do you love this one and dislike that one? It is emotion. So you love your son even if he is dull, because you love him with your emotion, and you love the clever son of your enemy with your intellect... Therefore the Almighty did not make emotion a field of legal obligation.

Our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), clarifies for us the matter of affection in his saying to his Companions, among whom was our master ʿUmar: this word lodged in the soul of ʿUmar. So he said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than my father and mother, or than my children and my wealth, but my own self, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah repeated it once more, until ʿUmar knew that it was a firm resolve. The Messenger of Allah surely intended a love other than the one ʿUmar was seeing; he intended rational love (al-hubb al-ʿaqli, love of the intellect and judgment). At that point ʿUmar said: "Now, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: now you have become dearer to me than my father and mother, dearer to me than my children and my wealth, and dearer to me than my own self that lies between my two sides.

So, the intended meaning of love for the Messenger of Allah is rational love. Were it not for him (ﷺ), we would not have been guided nor reached guidance, and were it not for him we would have perished. Thus you love Muhammad (ﷺ) as you love a bitter medicine: you love him not with your emotion but with your intellect. For this reason our master ʿUmar understood that the love required by the Sharia is love of the intellect, even if it afterwards turns into emotion and passionate attachment to the Essence, and this is another, higher degree than the first.

The Noble Qur'an teaches us this in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. That is: hatred for a people should not drive you to wrong them and to refrain from being just with them. So, hatred is not forbidden, because it is a matter of emotion: love whom you wish and hate whom you wish, but beware lest love or hatred lead you to wrong, by favouring the one you love and wronging the one you hate.

And because emotions are of this form, that is, they have no discipline within the self, they fall outside the scope of the legal obligations (al-taklif al-shar'i), for you do not know why emotion has inclined you to love or to hate.

When we reflect on the senses, the instincts and emotion, we find that the senses are a manifest, known phenomenon: the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on. Likewise the instincts are manifest in their effects and causes: when you are hungry you seek food, and when you long for your family you yearn for them. As for emotion, it is something hidden and not apparent, so the Qur'an gives it an example not from man, nor even from what is below him among animals or plants, but from inanimate matter. Consider His saying about the end of the disbelievers, the people of Pharaoh: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them...﴾ [al-Dukhan: 29].

It is well known that weeping is an emotional manifestation. Does the heaven weep? Does the earth weep? Yes, they weep and are affected, as if they are saying to these people: "Go, unmourned." Otherwise, Allah would not have negated weeping from them. And why should we find that far-fetched? The heavens and the earth are creatures of Allah, subject to subjugation (al-taskhir). Did not the True One, glory be to Him, say: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44]?

So it is no wonder that inanimate matter rejoices when it finds someone who glorifies alongside it and harmonizes with the glorifying cosmos, and no wonder that it grieves and weeps when humans deviate from this glorifying system. Accordingly, it may be said that the heaven and the earth did not weep over the destruction of the people of Pharaoh, and rejoiced at the guidance of Aasiya, the wife of Pharaoh. So, the heaven and the earth have emotion and affection: they love and hate, and they weep and rejoice.

This meaning was clarified for us by the Imam ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, when he said: "When the believer dies, two places weep over him: a place in the heaven and a place on the earth. As for his place in the heaven, it is the ascent of his deeds, which weeps for him because it has been deprived of the ascent of the good word and righteous deed. As for his place on the earth, it is his prayer-place," meaning: the place where he used to pray.

This was a necessary introduction with which we enter upon the story of our master Lot, in the saying of Allah the Exalted:
﴿And indeed Lot was among the messengers. When We saved him...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 37, verses 130–132 (part 1 of 3):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 127]. This is like the case of every nation to which the messengers came to bring them out of darkness into light. The messengers are necessarily denied: they are denied by the people of corruption and those who profit from corruption, and they are denied by the chiefs and great ones of the people, so that their leadership, their tyranny and their enslavement of the weak may continue. ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 127], meaning: they will be brought before Us for reckoning, the angels of punishment will bring them forth. The meaning is: do not think that you will escape from Our hands, for you have a return and a coming back, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115].

And His saying: ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 128], meaning: those whom He chose for His obedience and purified for His worship. Then this brief account of this noble Prophet is concluded with what the preceding one was concluded with: ﴿And We left for him among later generations. Peace be upon Ilyasin. Indeed, that is how We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾ [al-Saffat: 129–132].

From this conclusion we understand that goodness is a branch of faith, meaning that he was only a doer of good because he was first a believer.

Thus the Qur'an summarised for us the story of this Prophet, and it made clear that he came with a matter of creed, not a matter of legal obligation. He came to correct for the people the foundation and the base upon which life is built. This is the task of the messengers from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, for Allah created Adam, the father of mankind, as a khalifah (vicegerent) on the earth. The meaning of khalifah on the earth is that he should carry out, on the earth, a task on behalf of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted.

So that he could carry out this task, Allah supplied him with attributes from among His attributes. These attributes are bestowed and lent, not intrinsic to the khalifah, and therefore the Creator can strip them away at any time. Allah, exalted, is the Necessary Existent, the Highest, and He is characterised by these attributes in His own essence. Allah is Powerful and gives you of His power a power; He is Wise and bestows upon you of His wisdom a wisdom with which you manage things; Allah is the Subduer and gives you a subduing power with which you restrain whoever is under your control so that their affairs may be set right; and He gives you a compassionate mercy with which you show kindness to the weak and the needy.

So then: among the attributes of the Truth, the Necessary Existent Most High, is that He gives us existence from His existence, indeed existences многократные in number according to the number of individuals and in successive likenesses. But He, glory be to Him, gives from the essential existence an accidental existence. If you look at the afflictions that befall people in their senses or in their limbs, you will find them willed by Allah, exalted, either in creation or in direction. Why? Because man, as his Creator has informed about him: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6–7].

We have given for this an example of a child with his father: if the father gave his child pocket money each month, you would find the child keen to meet his father only once a month; but if he gave it to him day by day, the child would present himself to him every day, pressing upon him and showing himself in order to take the allowance to which he had become accustomed. You would see him, for instance, pass by his father in the morning and say: "Father, I am going to school." It is need that drove him to his father's affection.

So then: we must interpret the philosophy of the needs that cause the outcome, and these needs are what compel you to your Lord. Reality confirms this, and we often see a person not turning to his Lord nor setting right what is between him and his Creator except when something in him has gone wrong and its means have become scarce for him, so he finds nothing but his Lord and says: "O Lord, O Allah."

So we say: the Creator bestows upon the khalifah of His attributes, but these bestowed attributes remain accidental and not permanent. Therefore man dies as a foetus, dies as a child, dies as a youth, a middle-aged man and an old man. This matter explains to us the noble hadith:

The pronoun may refer back to Allah, exalted, and the meaning would be: Allah created Adam in His image, not in His reality. There is a difference between image and reality: the image is a snapshot taken of you in a particular form, which then freezes in that form. So this creation does not mean that Adam took from the attributes of Allah in reality, but in image, because reality has permanence, whereas the attributes in Adam have no permanence.

The pronoun may also refer back to Adam, and the meaning would be: Allah created Adam in his image, that is, in Adam's own image; for Allah, exalted, did not create Adam as a foetus, then he was born, then became a child, then a youth; rather He created him at the very beginning in this way, in the familiar form of the complete human, with complete limbs and members. So both interpretations are possible.

There is a difference between one who creates and one who creates a creator. To clarify this point, we say: a small child cannot, for instance, move a table from its place, whereas a strong man can move it for him; in this case he has not transferred his strength to the weak one so that he might act by himself, but has transferred to him the effect of his attribute, so he carries for him and lifts for him, while the child remains weak and unable to carry.

So we say: the aspect of greatness in the creation and giving of Allah is that He, glory be to Him, creates strength from His strength and gives it to you, so that you act by yourself and work with your hand; the creatures volunteer and help the weak and act on his behalf, but he remains weak; whereas the Creator, glory be to Him, gives the weak strength so that he acts by himself.

But be aware that these attributes are bestowed upon you, not intrinsic in you; for you are not essential in existence but a khalifah, and you must remain in the embrace of the One who made you khalifah, and beware of deviating from Him who made you khalifah, otherwise He will withdraw from you the components of this vicegerency.

When you see people of trials and disabilities, this one blind and this one lame, and so on, know that the Creator, glory be to Him, wants to draw your attention to Him and to alert you to the fact that you are not essential in existence but entrusted, and that you are something only as long as He who made you khalifah is with you; if He leaves you, you are nothing. The affliction of man in the universe is that he regards himself as essential; had he understood his role and the reality of his existence, affairs would have been set right.

Some look upon these disabilities as a disfigurement of creation and see no wisdom in them, but the truth is that they were created for a wisdom willed by Allah, exalted, and they are nothing but a means of illustration for people, so that they do not become deceived by sound limbs, and so that they remain mindful of Allah the Creator. And, as we have said, need is what compels you.

We see, for example, traffic policemen take a new car that has been smashed and place it in a conspicuous spot that people can see, so that drivers are deterred from recklessness in speed. This car is a means of illustration and a model placed there for a purpose, and perhaps they deliberately destroyed the car because of what results from the destruction of one car: the salvation of millions of cars.

Likewise, you who are healthy: when you see people with disabilities, say: "Praise be to Allah who has preserved me from what He has afflicted him with," and turn your attention to the blessings of Allah upon you, of which you often remain heedless. If you say: "What is the fault of this afflicted one, that Allah should make him a means of illustration for others?"

We say: if you realised what he has found as compensation for what he has lost, you would wish to be like him. Therefore we observe that people with disabilities are compensated by Allah with another quality that makes up for the defect within them; hence we say in proverbs: "Every person with a disability is a tyrant." You have seen the one with no forearms threading a needle with his feet, and the blind child who memorised the whole Qur'an at the age of six: Allah took sight from him and gave him insight. These are gifts that the healthy cannot attain.

We have already said that if a person with a withered arm struck you with his withered hand, you would know it to be a deadly blow, for it is a resting hand that does not work, so it contains a strength that the sound hand does not have, and when it is provoked all its strength is in that hand.

We say to our brothers whom Allah has afflicted with loss of sight: "Treasuries of knowledge!" Why? Because they acquire from knowledge what the sighted cannot attain; for the sighted is preoccupied by the many sights around him, whereas the blind is preoccupied by nothing, so the focus of his attention is always empty and ready to receive. Moreover, he cannot read by himself, so he seizes the opportunity to have things read to him, listens attentively, and understands what he hears so well that he does not need to have it repeated; therefore one of them said:

"I was born blind, and intelligence is among what blindness gives; so I came, with a marvellous hope, to knowledge as a refuge.
The light of the eye was lost, and the heart became a companion to knowledge, which, when people waste it, the heart gathers."

So then: when we see people with disabilities or afflictions, we look at our own completeness and do not look at the gifts with which they have been compensated in other respects. We have already said that the one who composed the famous world symphony was deaf!! And Timur-lenk, who bewildered the world and was known for his conquests, was lame!!

The true believer, when he sees others whom Allah has afflicted, does not look down upon them nor boast over them with the soundness of his limbs; rather he humbles himself before them, knowing that this deficiency is matched by a compensation, and he says to himself: "I wonder in which aspects they surpass me and distinguish themselves from me?" And with this outlook, all are made equal.

We say: a person must always remain mindful of this truth, that he is a khalifah of Allah in the universe and not essential in it. This vicegerency is like agency when you appoint someone to do a specific thing: if he regards himself as an agent in everything, the agency is corrupted. Therefore we see wise people, when they appoint others, appoint them according to the measure of need and necessity, so that the agency is not exploited and the agent does not overpower the owner of the essential right.

The good of the whole world and the rectitude of people's affairs rest upon this principle, the principle of vicegerency. The basic state of man is to remain a khalifah in need of the One who made him khalifah, and it is the habit that independence makes you forget, while need compels you and inclines you towards the One who made you khalifah.

When Allah created Adam to be a khalifah on the earth, did He send him down into existence to exercise his task of building up the earth and drawing out the secrets of Allah in the universe without preparing him for this task? How could He, when we take, for instance, the player whom we prepare simply to play: we train him, teach him, spend on him, and correct his mistakes until he reaches the required level; so what of the task of building up the earth?

Likewise, the Truth, exalted and glorified, trained Adam for this task, and settled him in a garden containing everything the soul desires: ﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it in abundance wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35].

Thus the Creator, glory be to Him, determined for Adam the manner of his livelihood in the Garden, permitting him to eat from it as he wished, with the exception of one tree. So the lawful is abundant and beyond counting, whereas the forbidden is limited; and likewise is Allah's way in life: the basic principle regarding things is permissibility, except what a text has prohibited, and that is confined to specific things.

Consider here this legislative precaution in His saying: ﴿And do not approach﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], and He did not say "do not eat." What is forbidden is merely approaching it, because closeness to the prohibited tempts you to it until you fall into it. Therefore you find the Qur'anic style in commands says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], whereas in prohibitions it says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

Therefore, when Islam prohibited wine, it did not merely forbid drinking it, but forbade everything connected with it: selling, buying, transporting, manufacturing, or even being present in a place where it is. Why? In order to block all the paths leading to it that entice one to it.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, makes clear to us the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and the prohibitions, He is drawing our attention to an important matter, as if He were saying to us: if you remain upright on Our method and Our obligation upon you, your life will remain sound without blemish, free of problems and hardships; but if you transgress these limits, then await the appearance of blemishes in society, whether they be social, moral, or economic, and so on.

In the story of Adam, peace be upon him, his eating from the tree is a symbolic indication of this matter. How? When Adam was upright upon the method of his Lord and committed himself to what Allah commanded him, he lived in the Garden in health, without nakedness; but when he disobeyed and obeyed the whispering of Satan, eating from the tree he had been forbidden, his private parts appeared for the first time, because while he was upright he was eating by the provision of his Lord, a provision in measure with the body's need and the components of life, so nothing remained over that would need to be expelled from the body.

But when desire intervened and he obeyed Satan, he spoiled the nutritional mixture prepared for him, so waste formed in his belly, and he felt for the first time a strange thing he had never known, and he was surprised to find an opening in his body from which something foul and foul-smelling came out.

Therefore Adam knew that this was a nakedness that must be covered, so he began to cut leaves from the trees to cover his nakedness and conceal his shame. This is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden. And their Lord called to them: Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

We have seen during wars that a soldier feeds on a small biscuit that performs the function of a meal, but leaves no waste in the body, so that the burden of supply is lightened, and the soldier has no need of the process of excretion.

So then: in the story of Adam and eating from the tree there is a symbolic allusion to the fact that while the commands of Allah are implemented, the condition of lands and servants is upright, and no nakedness or evils appear in society. Therefore, when you see in society a nakedness that has appeared in any sphere, whether scientific, economic, social, or moral, and so on, know that some clause of the method of Allah has been suspended; seek it out and try to repair it yourself first, if repair is within your power. Hence the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11].

Adam, peace be upon him, fell into this violation after Allah had made clear to him what was permitted to him and what was forbidden to him, and had made clear to him Satan's enmity, which was an enmity established from the time Allah commanded him to prostrate and he did not prostrate. Nevertheless, Adam listened to the whisper of Satan, though he should have made use of the blessing of intellect and reflected upon what his enemy Iblis had said when he said: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals﴾ [al-A'raf: 20].

That is, whoever eats from this tree becomes immortal and does not die. So then, why did you not eat from it yourself, O Iblis, if the matter is as you say? Did you not say to Allah, exalted: ﴿Reprieve me until the day they are resurrected﴾ [al-A'raf: 14]? Here is an indication of the obligation to reflect upon the whisper of Satan and not to submit to him.

So then: the period of Adam's residence in the Garden was a period of training in the method of vicegerency. When the violation occurred and disobedience took place, Allah willed to bring him out of the Garden and send him down into the life of the earth, to move in it with the movement of a khalifah, taking along the lesson of the earlier experience.

It is as if Allah were saying to him: take of the lawful what you wish, keep away from the unlawful, and beware of Satan, for he is your enemy, and he will continue to whisper to you in order to bring you into violation as he brought you into the first violation. So beware of listening to him, for if you listen to him, while he is your enemy, he will drive you out from a life of bliss into a life of misery, just as he drove you out of the Garden of adherence to a command and adherence to a prohibition: ﴿So We said: O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden, for you would be miserable﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. He did not say "you two would be miserable."

Here, al-Sha'rawi places within this verse a symbolic indication from the very beginning of creation, to resolve for us a question the world still discusses and will continue to discuss: the question of women going out to work and equality with men, and that a woman wants to establish her own identity... etc.

It is strange that a woman should demand more responsibilities. She wants to take on the man's task, while the man will not take anything from her task and will not bear any of her burdens. The man does not carry, does not give birth, and does not breastfeed. So you, woman, have taken on the man's task in addition to your own particular task, which he does not perform, and this is an injustice to women.

God's words to Adam, ﴿[then] you will suffer hardship﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], show from the beginning of creation that hardship, toil, work, and bearing responsibility are the man's task, and that the woman is mistress of her home, honored and esteemed. This image has remained inherited in our societies without distortion and without erasure. Even now, when a young man comes to propose to a girl, the head of the family makes a condition of him, saying: "Ente hatestetha wala hatshaghilha" (are you going to keep her as a dignified lady in her home, or will you take her out to work?).

Some say: how could Adam disobey, when he is a prophet? Then he is like Satan: this one disobeyed and that one disobeyed. We say: Adam disobeyed while he was in the period of training, in which the one who errs is not held to account, but rather he is corrected without being held accountable. The pupil at school has his mistake corrected by the teacher in red ink without being held to account for it, until the end-of-year examination comes, and then he is held accountable for the mistake.

So when Adam erred, he was in the period of training, and God corrected his error. Then he was not a prophet during this period, because Adam was created to be the father of all mankind, and mankind would be divided into two parts: a part chosen (mustafa), who are the messengers, and a part [who are] those to whom the messengers are sent, who are the ones who are chosen over (musṭafā ʿalayhi).

So: Adam at the beginning represented both parts. His experience represented the disobedience of mankind and the infallibility of the prophets. Therefore he erred, and God corrected him. Then he repented, so God accepted his repentance and chose him, and so it is with mankind. Read: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]; this is an indication of what would come to pass from mankind. ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122].

So: divine choosing (ijtiba') and infallibility came after the first experience, because Adam represented everyone: he represented the disobedience of mankind and he represented the infallibility of the prophets.

This vicegerent (khalifa) was given existence in advance, before he came into being. It is not that God created him, then looked at what he wanted and what he needed, and then created him, glory be to Him, in a creation suited to carrying out his task of building up the earth: ﴿He brought you into being from the earth and made you its settlers﴾ [Hud: 61].

The Mighty and Majestic has not made the essential acts of worship, that is, the pillars of Islam, the whole movement of life. Rather, He has made them the charge (shuhna) that helps you in the movement of life. Therefore, whoever says that Islam is just these pillars, which one performs and that is all, we say to him: No. Because these pillars draw strength from God through them, so that you may succeed in the movement of life. Islam is far broader than these five, as is shown by God's words in Surah al-Jumu'ah: ﴿O you who believe! When the call is proclaimed for the prayer on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trading﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9].

So: He called them and took them away from business and work, which is the summit of the movement of life, namely trading (bay'). Although trading is linked to buying (shira'), trading is stronger, so He singled it out for mention and did not say "leave off trading and buying." Why? They said: because He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of human nature, and He knows that man is reluctant when it comes to buying, not keen on it, but he is keen on selling and strives for it. So when the people of the house ask you to buy something, you may procrastinate in buying it or postpone it, and you are pleased when you go and find the shop closed. But if you were a seller, you would be most eager to sell. Why? Because the buyer spends and the seller receives. So the Mighty and Majestic mentioned trading because it is the fruit of the movement.

After the prayer ends, He said: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse through the land and seek of Allah's bounty...﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. So: taking you to prayer is a form of work, and He returned you after the prayer to work and striving.

When you reflect on the wording of the hadith (prophetic saying): i.e., these five are the pillars upon which Islam stands, and the building is other than the foundation it is built upon. Is the building we live in made only of the foundation and the columns? So: Islam is not the five pillars; rather Islam is broader than that. The pillars are the charge (shuhna) to which your Lord summons you, so you take from meeting Him the support that helps you carry out the movement of life.

We illustrate this with the battery: when you take it to be charged, we do not benefit from it during the charging period; rather, we give it the charge it needs so that it can work afterward.

Among the wonders of divine mercy is that God made going to the charge of human energy an obligatory duty that you must perform. You must meet Me five times a day and night, because you are My creation and My handiwork, and the maker knows best what repairs his handiwork. Imagine a piece of workmanship presented to its maker five times a day and night: would any defect remain in it? This is the case with a maker who is a human; how much more so with the Maker who is the Lord of mankind and their Creator, glory be to Him.

A human maker repairs his handiwork with a material thing, such as a nail or a spare part, for example. But the Creator, glory be to Him, repairs you without any material thing, because the engineer and his handiwork are material, so he repairs with material. But the Creator, glory be to Him, is the unseen (ghayb). So when He repairs a defect in you, He repairs it through the unseen, so you neither feel it nor see it.

So: we say that one must understand religion as it truly is, and understand that each of us has a task. If someone else excels over you, know that his excellence is for your benefit and returns to you, because through his excellence he provides a service to you, while he does not benefit from you. Whoever is skilled at a craft certainly benefits himself and benefits others, unlike the one who is skilled at nothing.

That is why we say among the peasants: "the carpenter's door is off its hinges" (bab al-najjar mukhala'). The carpenter's skill appears when he makes things for others, because he receives a wage; but he does not practise his craft for himself. So: when you see one who excels over you, do not envy him or bear him a grudge; rather, wish him more, and wish him good. Something of this good will certainly reach you, and this excellence will return to you in the form of a service he provides for you.

That is why, when we were peasants, if one of us lost a cow or a buffalo, everyone would grieve, to the extent that once we saw a group weeping over a calf that had died, and we were surprised. People weep over a dead person among them, but over an animal?! Afterwards we came to know that this calf was the one that turns the water-wheel (saqiya) and ploughs the land from which these people eat, and the good of this land reaches them. In the countryside we did not buy cucumbers, molokhia, okra, and much else; rather, it was given as a gift and was not sold.

So: the gift extended among creatures returns to all creatures. When you see someone who excels, bless him, and when you see someone who is skilled at work that you are not skilled at, do not bear him a grudge, because you will need him to do your work well, even if you dislike him or are at odds with him. You are keen on him to work for you, because you know how skilled he is at the work, so you go to him out of concern for your own interest. In this way the required balance in society is achieved, and the affairs of creatures are set right on a foundation of need.

If you reflect on yourself, as God said: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21], you will find in yourself this balance between the organs. For example, you have the right hand, with which you perform certain tasks that suit it, and the left hand, with which you perform other tasks that suit it. The right hand is for noble, honored tasks, while the left is for what is less than that. The right is usually stronger than the left, more active, and more precise in handling.

Consider, for example, when you want to trim your nails: you trim the left hand with the right, and the cutting comes out precise and comfortable, unlike cutting the right with the left. So: the right hand's ability benefits the left, and the left's lack of ability benefits the right. This draws our attention to the fact that perfections in the universe are perfections that spread through it, like the spreading of water.

When God, glory be to Him, created the human vicegerent, He gave him formations suited to his task. The first of these formations are the organs that we call the senses, through which we perceive things, which they call the five outward senses. Their saying "outward" is a precaution against senses that will be discovered and that science knows; indeed, other senses beyond the five have been discovered in humans, such as the sense by which I know hunger, the sense of distance (hassat al-bayn) by which I distinguish the distance between two things, and the sense of muscle (hassat al-adala) by which I know the weight of things.

When you reflect on these five known senses, you find that the legal obligation (taklif shar'i) came in accordance with this formation of the senses. Each sense in a human has a function, and each organ has a task. The performance by each organ of its task is called "action" ('amal). The heart acts through intention, the tongue speaks, the ear hears, the nose smells, the hand touches things, and the eye sees. All of this is action.

Here we must distinguish between 'amal (action) and fi'l (deed), and deed is opposed by speech (qawl), which is the task of the tongue. So God said: ﴿O you who believe! Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2].

So: speech, which is the task of the tongue, took one part alone, and the rest of the senses took the other part. Speech belongs to the tongue, and deeds belong to the remaining senses. Why did the tongue take one share and the remaining senses the other? They said: because speech is the means of conveying from us what the messengers require, so that we may do it, and of conveying our requests from others so that they may do them.

So: all deeds are in the service of speech, and God's method does not come to us except through speech, which carries the command to the senses so that they act. And action is not necessarily physical labour; it may be inward action, such as the action of the heart, which is intention, as we have said. The Shari'a (sacred law) governs these senses and defines for them the framework within which they act, in light of what is permitted (halal) and forbidden (haram).

The task of the senses is to pick up perceptions and then present them to the intellect, which refines them with true refinement, by comparing them and knowing that this suits such-and-such and that suits such-and-such. After this refinement, it hands them over to the heart so that they become a belief (aqida) in it. The word 'aqida means a thing that is tied and cannot be untied, and is not presented for debate again in the intellect. For example, a small child is attracted by the beautiful shape of fire, so he tries to grasp it, and the fire burns him, and for the first time he feels heat. So a belief or intellectual principle forms in him that fire burns, and he does not approach it afterwards, and he continues all his life following this belief or this principle, without needing to test it again.

When this belief settles in the heart, the heart pumps it with the blood, so it travels through the whole body and permeates all the organs, and they absorb it. This explains for us the noble hadith... Then, after God, glory be to Him, gave man the organs and senses, He created the instincts (ghara'iz), which are matters necessary for you, fixed in your make-up, and you cannot dispense with them. But this instinct may press upon you and take you away from its purpose, and then the Shari'a must intervene to restrain its excess and return it to the balance for which God created it.

The Shari'a intervenes to elevate the instinct and refine it, not to suppress it and eliminate it. Eating is an instinct for preserving life, and what our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said suffices concerning it: "...and it should not go beyond that and turn into gluttony and excess." Curiosity is an instinct that God made for exploring His secrets in the universe and reflecting on His creatures. If it goes beyond this framework and becomes spying and tracking people's private faults, it has strayed from its task, and here the Shari'a intervenes to elevate it and return it to its balance.

The most fierce of human instincts is the sexual instinct, especially in youth. God made this instinct for preserving the species and continuing offspring. This is the task for which the sexual instinct was created, and the Shari'a has been keen to preserve this instinct accompanied by a method of its movement for those who created it, so that affairs may be set right, because offspring is the first wealth that must be preserved, so that the offspring may come noble and pure.

We have previously distinguished between legitimate offspring, attributed to the two parents, and illegitimate offspring, and how the former is met with joy, tenderness, compassion, and care, while the latter is met with hatred and unwillingness, and perhaps its mother thinks of getting rid of it, even by throwing it onto the street.

From here, religion has been keen to build the family on a sound foundation, with honour, dignity, and self-respect, under the shade of God's word and His method, which secures for you the safety of your lineage, so that it comes trustworthy, something you can rely on, which you care for, and which you raise in the best way. This is the aim of the Shari'a.

We have previously spoken about the difference between the lawful and the unlawful in this matter, and mentioned the noble hadith... So: this instinct is created in human nature for performing a task, and so that it remains within the framework for which it was created. But the reality is that many people take it out of its purpose. It is strange that a person should wrong the animal in this matter, when he says: "This is animal lust," and boasts of it.

This statement shows a lack of understanding of the animal's instinct, because the animal stops at the limits of its instinct as God created it. That is why we have never seen a female animal that conceived and then allowed a male to mount her afterwards. Likewise, the male sniffs her, knows that she is pregnant, and turns away from her.

Is this animal lust in the sense that we mean by this word? No, rather it is human... You may compare this instinct in the animal and in the human, and you will see the wonder of humans' departure from its intended purpose.

Among the wisdom of the Creator, glory be to Him, is that He linked the sexual instinct and offspring with enjoyment. This is because offspring has demands, consequences, and responsibilities. If there were no pleasure to encourage the human, he would shun the matter and turn away from it.

The Almighty, glory be to Him, deals with the believers according to one method, with contrasting matters such as honour and humiliation. The believer is not disposed to constant honour nor to constant humiliation; rather, the situation he lives in dictates to him whether he should be honourable or humble. So humility and submission are for his fellow believers, and honour and haughtiness are towards the disbelieving deniers, as God said describing our master, the Messenger of Allah, and the believers: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; and those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves...﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

So: they are firm and merciful at the same time, and this is evidence that the believer is not governed by his instincts except according to the measures of the Creator of instincts.

Also among the formations in the creation of man, after the senses and instincts, is that God created in man emotion (ʿatifa), and emotion is a feeling whose cause we do not know. That is why you meet a person and feel at ease with him, and another whom you dislike, just like that, without any prior dealing. Why then do you love this one and dislike that one? It is emotion. So you love your son even if he is dull, because you love him with your emotion, and you love the clever son of your enemy with your intellect... Therefore the Almighty did not make emotion a field of legal obligation.

Our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), clarifies for us the matter of affection in his saying to his Companions, among whom was our master ʿUmar: this word lodged in the soul of ʿUmar. So he said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than my father and mother, or than my children and my wealth, but my own self, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah repeated it once more, until ʿUmar knew that it was a firm resolve. The Messenger of Allah surely intended a love other than the one ʿUmar was seeing; he intended rational love (al-hubb al-ʿaqli, love of the intellect and judgment). At that point ʿUmar said: "Now, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: now you have become dearer to me than my father and mother, dearer to me than my children and my wealth, and dearer to me than my own self that lies between my two sides.

So, the intended meaning of love for the Messenger of Allah is rational love. Were it not for him (ﷺ), we would not have been guided nor reached guidance, and were it not for him we would have perished. Thus you love Muhammad (ﷺ) as you love a bitter medicine: you love him not with your emotion but with your intellect. For this reason our master ʿUmar understood that the love required by the Sharia is love of the intellect, even if it afterwards turns into emotion and passionate attachment to the Essence, and this is another, higher degree than the first.

The Noble Qur'an teaches us this in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. That is: hatred for a people should not drive you to wrong them and to refrain from being just with them. So, hatred is not forbidden, because it is a matter of emotion: love whom you wish and hate whom you wish, but beware lest love or hatred lead you to wrong, by favouring the one you love and wronging the one you hate.

And because emotions are of this form, that is, they have no discipline within the self, they fall outside the scope of the legal obligations (al-taklif al-shar'i), for you do not know why emotion has inclined you to love or to hate.

When we reflect on the senses, the instincts and emotion, we find that the senses are a manifest, known phenomenon: the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on. Likewise the instincts are manifest in their effects and causes: when you are hungry you seek food, and when you long for your family you yearn for them. As for emotion, it is something hidden and not apparent, so the Qur'an gives it an example not from man, nor even from what is below him among animals or plants, but from inanimate matter. Consider His saying about the end of the disbelievers, the people of Pharaoh: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them...﴾ [al-Dukhan: 29].

It is well known that weeping is an emotional manifestation. Does the heaven weep? Does the earth weep? Yes, they weep and are affected, as if they are saying to these people: "Go, unmourned." Otherwise, Allah would not have negated weeping from them. And why should we find that far-fetched? The heavens and the earth are creatures of Allah, subject to subjugation (al-taskhir). Did not the True One, glory be to Him, say: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44]?

So it is no wonder that inanimate matter rejoices when it finds someone who glorifies alongside it and harmonizes with the glorifying cosmos, and no wonder that it grieves and weeps when humans deviate from this glorifying system. Accordingly, it may be said that the heaven and the earth did not weep over the destruction of the people of Pharaoh, and rejoiced at the guidance of Aasiya, the wife of Pharaoh. So, the heaven and the earth have emotion and affection: they love and hate, and they weep and rejoice.

This meaning was clarified for us by the Imam ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, when he said: "When the believer dies, two places weep over him: a place in the heaven and a place on the earth. As for his place in the heaven, it is the ascent of his deeds, which weeps for him because it has been deprived of the ascent of the good word and righteous deed. As for his place on the earth, it is his prayer-place," meaning: the place where he used to pray.

This was a necessary introduction with which we enter upon the story of our master Lot, in the saying of Allah the Exalted:
﴿And indeed Lot was among the messengers. When We saved him...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 37, verse 133:

The mission of Sayyidina Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, in calling his people was the most arduous of missions; for this reason he is mentioned in the Qur'an seventeen times, in the nominative and the genitive, and ten times in the accusative. The difficulty of his mission, peace be upon him, lay in the fact that he came to correct the most violent of the instincts in the human soul, which is the sexual instinct.

If only this instinct had been among his people in its natural course, meaning the instinct of a man towards a woman. Rather, it was a deviant sexual instinct that had no precedent before, namely the relationship of a man with a man. Therefore there came from them a crime and an abominable deed, novel, which no one before them had committed, as Allah the Exalted said on the tongue of Sayyidina Lut: ﴿Do you commit the abomination that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80].

We have said previously: every one of us has, in his own particular self, a freedom; when it passes to others, restrictions come upon this freedom. So: I have a freedom with myself, I have a freedom with my family, and I have a freedom with people in general in the street, and each has limits and obligations. A person, for example, when he closes his private room upon himself, his freedom is at its widest, since no one is with him to limit his freedom.

When he goes out from his private room to the hall, for example, his freedom becomes somewhat restricted by the presence of his family and children. When he goes out to the street, where the common people are, his freedom is restricted more; because everyone he deals with in the street has a freedom, and the freedom of others restricts your freedom. When you go to the club, for example, where the beloved ones and friends are, you go with your complete attire and your abundant courtesy... etc.

Therefore the boldness of the people of Lut in their indecency appeared, to the extent that they used to commit it in their club, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you commit the evil in your gatherings﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], meaning: the act that you should not do, which you do in seclusion, you do openly in the club. This act is prohibited by the Shari'a, even if it is with a wife who is lawful to you; because coming to the wife is only in the place of begetting offspring.

Therefore, when some called for a man's freedom to enjoy a woman wherever he wishes, understanding this freedom from the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth however you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], we say to them: you have overlooked the meaning of "tilth" here. The tilth is the land prepared for growing; likewise, coming to the wife is in the place of growing, where the child comes. If it is in the other place, where there is no growing, it is forbidden. If Islam prohibits this act with the wife, how much more so if one does it with a man like himself?

And just as the Shari'a prohibited the deed of the people of Lut, which is a man coming to a man, it likewise prohibited that a woman do it with a woman, which is what is called sihaq (lesbianism), and we seek refuge with Allah; and this prohibition is by analogy with the man.

So: the Shari'a corrected the deviant instincts in the relationship of a man with a man, and in the relationship of a woman with a woman, and in the marital relationship between a husband and his wife, and it set deterrent controls in this matter. Why? Because this deviation will harm the progeny and the building up of the universe, and the Almighty wishes for His vicegerent on earth to come pure and noble, so that he may be worthy of this vicegerency.

Therefore Sayyidina Lut, peace be upon him, is mentioned twenty-seven times, for the weight of the mission with which he was charged. Whereas Sayyidina Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, despite his importance in the procession of the messages, and despite the wondrous nature of his creation, is mentioned twenty-five times.

And I personally have taken issue with many writers and scholars who attribute this crime, and attribute its perpetrator, to the Prophet of Allah Lut, peace be upon him; they say of the abominable deed "lawat" (sodomy) and of its perpetrator "lūṭī" (a Lutist), and this is a gross error and a great fault that we should attribute ugliness and indecency to the Prophet of Allah, who came to fight it and to correct people's conduct regarding it...

That is: "qawm Lut" (the people of Lut) is the idiomatic phrase, but in the language there is what is called naḥt (coining a compound), and from the word one may coin what indicates that the people are the practitioners of this deed, apart from Lut, peace be upon him; it is a fault to make him the banner of this indecency.

These verses before us mention the story of Sayyidina Lut with his people; they are a concise snapshot of the end of the story and its conclusion, where Allah saved the believers and destroyed the disbelievers. The beginning of Lut's story, when he met his paternal uncle Sayyidina Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, is as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Lut believed in him, and he said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord; indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26].

So this is a snapshot of the story, and not a repetition of it as some claim, for the stories in the Qur'an do not come as one continuous narration; rather they come as different snapshots, which it mentions in their appropriate occasions...

The mission of Prophet Lot (ﷺ)... [start of passage text] — Prophet Lot's mission in calling his people was the most arduous of missions. For this reason he is mentioned in the Qur'an seventeen times in the nominative and genitive cases, and ten times in the accusative, and the difficulty of his mission, peace be upon him, lay in the fact that he came to correct the most violent of the instincts of the human soul, which is the sexual instinct.

Would that this instinct... Among his people it had been in its natural course, meaning the instinct of a man toward a woman. Rather, it was a deviant sexual instinct the like of which had never existed before, namely the relationship of a man with a man. Therefore there came from them a crime and an abominable act, novel, that no one other than them had committed before, as the Exalted said on the tongue of Prophet Lot: ﴿Do you commit an abomination that no one in the worlds has committed before you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80].

We have said earlier that each one of us has freedom in his own self. When that freedom moves to another, there come restrictions on this freedom. So: I have freedom with myself, I have freedom with my family, and I have freedom from people in general in the street, and each has limits and obligations. A person, for example, when he closes his private room upon himself, his freedom is wider, since no one is with him to limit his freedom.

If he goes out of his private room to the living room, for example, his freedom becomes somewhat restricted because of the presence of his family and children. If he goes out to the street, where ordinary people are, his freedom is restricted more, because everyone he deals with in the street has a freedom, and the freedom of others restricts your freedom. If you go to the club, for example, where loved ones and friends are, you go in your complete attire and your refined manners... etc.

Therefore the boastfulness of the people of Lot in their abomination appeared, to the point that they would practise it in their club, as the Exalted said: ﴿and in your gatherings you commit the evil﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], meaning: the act that you should not do, which you do in private, you do openly in the club. This act is forbidden by the Shari'ah, even if it were with the wife who is lawful to you, because intercourse with a wife is only to be in the place of procreation.

Therefore, when some called for a man's freedom to enjoy a woman wherever he wishes, understanding this freedom from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth however you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], we say to them: you have overlooked the meaning of "tilth" here. Tilth is land prepared for growing. Likewise, intercourse with a wife is to be in the place of growth, where the child comes. If it is in the other place, where there is no growth, it is forbidden. If Islam forbids this act with a wife, then what about if one does it with a man like himself?

Just as the Shari'ah forbade the act of the people of Lot, which is a man's coming to a man, it likewise forbade a woman doing it with a woman, which is called *al-siḥāq* (lesbianism), God forbid, and this prohibition is by analogy with the man.

So: the Shari'ah corrected the deviant instincts in a man's relationship with a man, in a woman's relationship with a woman, and in the marital relationship between husband and wife, and set deterrent controls in this matter. Why? Because this deviation would harm the progeny and the building of the universe, and the Truthful, glorified is He, wants His vicegerent on earth to come pure and noble, so that he may be fit for this vicegerency.

Therefore Prophet Lot, peace be upon him, is mentioned twenty-seven times, because of the weight of the mission he was charged with. Whereas Prophet Jesus, peace be upon him, despite his importance in the procession of messages and despite the wondrous nature of his creation, is mentioned twenty-five times.

Personally, I have taken issue with many writers and scholars who attribute this crime, and attribute its perpetrator, to the Prophet of God Lot, peace be upon him. They say of the abominable act "lawāṭ" (sodomy) and of its perpetrator "lūṭī" (sodomite). This is a grave error and a serious fault, that we attribute ugliness and abomination to the Prophet of God, who came to fight it and to correct people's conduct regarding it. They said: we proceed in this according to the requirement of Arabic speech in attribution, as the versifier said:

*And mention the singular when referring to a group, if it does not resemble a singular in form.*

That is, they are the people of Lot by attribution. But in the language there is what is called *al-naḥt* (forming a single word by blending/composition), and from the word we can coin what conveys that the people are the doers of this act, far from Lot, peace be upon him. It is a fault that we make him the title for this abomination.

These verses before us mention the story of Prophet Lot with his people. They are a concise snapshot of the end of the story and its conclusion, where God saved the believers and destroyed the disbelievers. The beginning of Lot's story is when he met his paternal uncle, Prophet Abraham, peace be upon them both, as the Exalted said: ﴿So Lot believed him, and he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord; indeed He is the Mighty, the Wise"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26].

This is a snapshot of the story, not a repetition of it as some claim. The stories in the Qur'an do not come as one continuous narrative; rather they come as different snapshots, mentioned on their occasions.

Shallow readers have stood at the matter of Moses' staff, accusing the Qur'an of repetition, and this is the result of their deficiency in understanding the Book of God. The first command to cast the staff was in the sphere of companionship, for the Truthful wished to make Moses undergo this experience between him and his Lord, as shown by the question of companionship: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17]. God knows what is in his hand, but He wished to make him at ease. Therefore Moses, peace be upon him, lengthened the answer, saying: ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean on it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18] Then God commanded him to cast it: ﴿He said, "Cast it, O Moses." So he cast it, and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly. He said, "Take it and do not fear; We will return it to its original form."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 19–21].

So: the Truthful wished to train Moses, so that when his encounter with Pharaoh came and he saw the staff as a real serpent, he would have had practice and would not fear. Then the command to cast the staff came the second time, in another situation, before Pharaoh and the sorcerers. So: this is one situation, and that is another situation.

We have said earlier that each one of us has freedom in his own self. When that freedom moves to another, there come restrictions on this freedom. So: I have freedom with myself, I have freedom with my family, and I have freedom from people in general in the street, and each has limits and obligations. If he goes out of his private room to the living room, for example, his freedom becomes somewhat restricted because of the presence of his family and children. If he goes out to the street, where ordinary people are, his freedom is restricted more, because everyone he deals with in the street has a freedom, and the freedom of others restricts your freedom. If you go to the club, for example, where loved ones and friends are, you go in your complete attire and your refined manners... etc.

Therefore the boastfulness of the people of Lot in their abomination appeared, to the point that they would practise it in their club, as the Exalted said: ﴿and in your gatherings you commit the evil﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], meaning: the act that you should not do, which you do in private, you do openly in the club. This act is forbidden by the Shari'ah, even if it were with the wife who is lawful to you, because intercourse with a wife is only to be in the place of procreation.

Therefore, when some called for a man's freedom to enjoy a woman wherever he wishes, understanding this freedom from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth however you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], we say to them: you have overlooked the meaning of "tilth" here. If Islam forbids this act with a wife, then what about if one does it with a man like himself?

Just as the Shari'ah forbade the act of the people of Lot, which is a man's coming to a man, it likewise forbade a woman doing it with a woman, which is called *al-siḥāq* (lesbianism), God forbid, and this prohibition is by analogy with the man.

So: the Shari'ah corrected the deviant instincts in a man's relationship with a man, in a woman's relationship with a woman, and in the marital relationship between husband and wife, and set deterrent controls in this matter. Why? Because this deviation would harm the progeny and the building of the universe, and the Truthful, glorified is He, wants His vicegerent on earth to come pure and noble, so that he may be fit for this vicegerency.

So: we say the Qur'anic narratives came, each snapshot in its occasion, to strengthen the Messenger of God, as the Exalted said: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have recited it in measured recitation﴾ [al-Furqan: 32].

He, the Glorified, says: ﴿And indeed Lot was among the messengers. When We saved him and his family, all of them, except an old woman among those who remained behind. Then We destroyed the others﴾ [al-Saffat: 133–136], that is: by overturning and stoning.

The word "wa-ahlahu" (and his family): "al-ahl" is applied to a man's closest kin, and it is applied to the wife. The Truthful and Exalted here informed that He saved Lot and his family, all of them, and excepted from them his wife: ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind﴾ [al-Saffat: 135]. In another verse He said: ﴿except your wife; she was among those who remained behind﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 33]. The "ghabirun" are the plural of "ghabir," and "ghabir" is applied to two opposite meanings. "Ghabir": the thing that has passed and ended, and "ghabir" meaning the remaining. Both meanings came together for the wife of Lot: she is among those who remained behind whom We left to perish, or among those who remained behind, meaning also remaining for punishment until it comes.

Then the Truthful reminds us that the story in the Qur'an is not told for entertainment, but for lesson and admonition, saying: ﴿And indeed you pass by them﴾ [al-Saffat: 137], that is, over their traces in Sodom, ﴿in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137], ﴿and by night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 138]. Yes, they pass by them in their journeys and travels and in their trade, in the winter and summer caravans, and they see their traces and what remains of their dwellings.

This was a concise snapshot and a swift telegram of the story of Prophet Lot with his people, and exactly like it is the story of Prophet Jonah:

﴿And indeed Jonah was among the messengers...﴾.

First, the Truth (may He be glorified) affirmed for our master Yunus (peace be upon him) that he is a messenger: ﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers﴾. So let us keep this idea in mind before entering his story, and let us understand the story within this framework. Then, if something happens from him that does not seem fitting for a messenger in your view, know that this does not discredit his status as a messenger. The One who sent him has testified to his prophethood, has not dismissed him from it, and has not stripped him of his station after what happened.

Therefore, when you hear his story, do not say that this act is not fitting for a messenger; for you are not more jealous for God than God Himself.
